Sample-Efficient Optimization over Generative Priors via Coarse Learnability

This work was done while the author was visiting Google Research.
Pranjal Awasthi Email: pranjalawasthi@google.com    Sreenivas Gollapudi Email: sgollapu@google.com    Ravi Kumar Email: ravi.k53@gmail.com Affiliation: Google Research, Mountain View, USA and
Department of Computer Science, Duke University, Durham, USA    Kamesh Munagala Email: kamesh@cs.duke.edu Affiliation: 
Abstract

We study zeroth-order optimization where solutions must minimize a cost d⁡(s)d(s) while maintaining high probability under a complex generative prior ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) (e.g., a parameterized model). This reduces to sampling from a target distribution proportional to ℒ(s)e−T⋅d(s)\mathcal{L}(s)e^{-T\cdot d(s)}. Since classical model-based optimization (MBO) lacks finite-sample guarantees for expressive approximate learners, we introduce coarse learnability, a flexible statistical assumption requiring only that a learned model covers the target’s probability mass within a polynomial factor.

Leveraging this assumption, we design an iterative MBO algorithm called ALDrIFT with a sample correction step that provably approximates the target using only a polynomial number of samples. We apply this framework to globally optimizing non-convex objectives bounded by a quadratic envelope in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, where we show this assumption is naturally satisfied for a family of “optimistic” posterior distributions. To reach global ε\varepsilon-optimality, this implies a sample complexity of O~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon), a rate characteristic of optimistic space-partitioning methods.

We further justify coarse learnability as an assumption for generative priors theoretically, proving that in simple settings, parametric maximum likelihood estimation and over-smoothed kernel density estimators naturally satisfy it.

Finally, one motivation for our framework comes from inference-time alignment. Though our primary contribution pertains to the theoretical foundations of MBO, we provide qualitative evidence that, in simple settings, even primitive LLMs can shift their distributions toward lower-cost regions when fine-tuned with zeroth-order feedback.

1 Introduction

Model-based optimization (MBO) is a broadly applicable framework for zeroth-order optimization: a probabilistic model over candidate solutions is iteratively updated using function evaluations, guiding search toward high-performing solutions. Classical MBO methods such as the cross-entropy method (Rubinstein, 1999) are well-studied and widely used, but their theoretical guarantees are asymptotic (as opposed to finite sample) and rely on strong structural assumptions. These assumptions break down when the generative model is an expressive approximate learner, such as a neural network, leaving the finite-sample behavior of MBO in this regime theoretically uncharacterized. As discussed more in Section 8, a motivating instance is inference-time optimization with learned generative priors, including language models, where one seeks to enforce global objectives while retaining high prior likelihood under the generative model. While analyzing MBO over modern generative models remains challenging, establishing finite-sample guarantees in tractable, continuous domains is a necessary first step. This requires more flexible assumptions on the generative model, which is the focus of this paper.

1.1 Model-Based Optimization (MBO) with a Generative Prior

We study a zeroth-order optimization framework, where the goal is to minimize a function d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) given only oracle access to its values. The function d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) might represent a continuous non-convex loss surface, or a discrete penalty for violating global constraints. To guide this search, we assume access to a generative prior ℒ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot) and our objective is to sample effectively from a target distribution of the form pT(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−T⋅d(s)p_{T}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-T\cdot d(s)}, where TT is a ‘temperature’ parameter. Samples from this distribution naturally balance low values of d⁡(s)d(s) with high probability under the prior ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s). This formulation is versatile: in continuous domains, the prior provides regularization to escape local minima (see Section 5); in combinatorial settings, it allows a division of labor where an external checker enforces global feasibility via d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) while a generative model enforces semantic priors via ℒ⁡(⋅)\mathcal{L}(\cdot).

Our primary object in this paper is sampling from pTp_{T}; approximate optimization of dd follows by choosing TT appropriately large. For such TT, the target distribution pTp_{T} can become exponentially far from the initial prior ℒ\mathcal{L}, making direct sampling or simple rejection-based corrections infeasible.

Sample-Efficient Model-Based Optimization. To address this sampling challenge, we adopt the perspective of model-based optimization (MBO), most notably the cross-entropy method (Rubinstein, 1999) and model reference adaptive search (Hu et al., 2007). (Sections 1.2 and A.2 contain a detailed comparison.) These methods, which are widely used for derivative-free non-convex optimization (Shahriari et al., 2016; Snoek et al., 2012), optimize an objective by iteratively updating a probabilistic or neural search distribution that concentrates on the optimum. However, classical guarantees for these methods typically rely on asymptotic convergence arguments via structural properties of specific surrogates, such as natural exponential families (Hu et al., 2007). These results do not extend to the finite-sample regime, either with well-structured priors or with generative models that function as approximate learners. Our work bridges this gap by providing polynomial sample complexity bounds for this class of algorithms under a general coarse learnability assumption, replacing rigid structural constraints with a statistical coverage condition.

Simulated Annealing and ALDrIFT. We operationalize this framework via ALDrIFT (Algorithm Driven Iterated Fitting of Targets), an iterative algorithm in which a generative model is progressively refined. We construct an intermediate distribution pτ(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−τ⋅d(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-\tau\cdot d(s)} and detail how ALDrIFT treats τ\tau as a (inverse) temperature parameter—drawing inspiration from simulated annealing (Kirkpatrick et al., 1983; Kalai and Vempala, 2006; Jerrum and Sinclair, 1996)—and gradually increases it to TT to assign more weight to the objective dd (see Section 3). Crucially, at each iteration, ALDrIFT performs a Metropolis–Hastings step to generate samples from the current target distribution pτ​(s)p_{\tau}(s), using the learned generative model as a proposal. In this setting, using importance (Thomas and Brunskill, 2016) or rejection sampling (Huang et al., 2025) would require exponentially many samples. Metropolis–Hastings circumvents this by relying solely on relative likelihood ratios, allowing the procedure to remain efficient even when the target and initial distributions differ exponentially.

The resulting samples are then used to fit the new generative model (via say parameter estimation) so that it produces samples that are more closely aligned with pτ​(s)p_{\tau}(s). At a high level, this approach is analogous to related methods in convex optimization (Kalai and Vempala, 2006), to approximate policy-iteration schemes from reinforcement learning (Schulman et al., 2015; Agarwal et al., 2020; Kakade and Langford, 2002; Peters and Schaal, 2007; Peters et al., 2010), and to sequential MCMC Del Moral et al. (2006); Cappé et al. (2004); Neal (1998); Andrieu et al. (2010), though the details and objectives differ. Further, as discussed in Section A.2, ALDrIFT is an instance of the model reference adaptive search (MRAS) framework (Hu et al., 2007), and our algorithm and analysis can be interpreted as a finite-sample robustification of MRAS via the Metropolis–Hastings proposal step.

Formal Guarantees via Coarse Learnability. Our main theoretical contribution in Section 4 is a proof that ALDrIFT converges to the target distribution pT​(s)p_{T}(s) with polynomial sample complexity, under a novel coverage assumption we call coarse learnability. (See Assumption 2 in Section 4 for a formal statement.) This assumption formalizes approximate learning as follows: given mm samples from a target distribution, we can learn a generative model whose density envelopes the target density within a factor of poly​(m)\mbox{poly}(m), except on an exponentially small error set.

A central conceptual contribution of our work is the formulation of coarse learnability itself. At a conceptual level, as discussed in Section 4, coarse learnability identifies a sufficient statistical condition under which any sampling-based learner can provably refine a generative model toward a target distribution. As we discuss in Section 1.2, coarse learnability is related to the notion of coverage in reinforcement learning (Szepesvári and Munos, 2005; Xie et al., 2023), which similarly quantifies when a policy explores enough of the optimal state-action space to permit efficient improvement. Coarse learnability differs by treating coverage as a dynamic statistical outcome of the model fitting instead of as a static assumption, regenerating the required coverage dynamically at each iteration.

Provable Bounds for Non-Convex Global Optimization. Section 4 gives a general finite-sample guarantee for ALDrIFT under Assumption 2. In Section 5, we show the utility of this result in the classical setting of ε\varepsilon-approximately globally optimizing a non-convex function in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, where prior results only show asymptotic convergence of MBO with infinitely many samples Hu et al. (2007). In contrast, we prove that on a well-studied class of quadratically bounded non-convex functions (Bubeck et al., 2011; Munos, 2011) with known curvature bounds, ALDrIFT is sample-efficient. Unlike existing MBO methods that fit an exact exponential family model, we fit a wider Gaussian posterior, analogous to optimistic exploration in bandit literature (Bubeck et al., 2011). This key difference enables us to verify Assumption 2 in this setting, and show that a strengthening of ALDrIFT achieves sample complexity O~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon), with dimension- and geometry-dependent constants. This rate is characteristic of optimistic space partitioning methods (Munos, 2011; Bubeck et al., 2011) (see Section 5 for some caveats) and is exponentially better than that achievable by local MCMC methods (Holley and Stroock, 1987; Hajek, 1988). We note that for this sample-complexity guarantee, Assumption 2 is no longer an assumption, as it is rigorously verified. Complementing our theory, we present an empirical demonstration of the need for the inflated proposal and sample correction steps with limited sample budgets in Section 7.

Theoretical Plausibility of Coarse Learnability.In Section 6, we present theoretical evidence justifying Assumption 2 for certain generative models. We demonstrate that standard MLE naturally induces the required coverage properties in several simplified settings: the agnostic setting where the model is misspecified (e.g., a unimodal learner approximating a multimodal target) and precise density approximation is impossible; for the realizable setting for well-behaved exponential families; and non-parametric settings such as standard Kernel Density Estimation.

Motivating Application: Inference-time Alignment. Though our primary focus is to theoretically formalize the mechanics of MBO under generative priors, we note in Section 8 that one motivating application is the combination (via inference-time alignment and fine-tuning) of classical combinatorial algorithms with generative models (Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Madaan et al., 2023) to solve problems that require both global feasibility and adherence to local priors: route planning with qualitative scenic preferences as prior, molecular design with learned drug-likeness priors, or scheduling with semantic session coherence. In such problems, the generative model encodes local constraints that a classical algorithm cannot capture, while the algorithm enforces global structure that a generative model cannot reliably guarantee. LLMs are a natural family of priors for this purpose, though, as we illustrate in Section 8, they can fail to enforce global combinatorial properties on their own, confirming the need for the hybrid approach.

We present qualitative results in Section 9 demonstrating that even a relatively primitive LLM can iteratively acquire combinatorial constraints (initially unknown to it) from only a few samples via fine-tuning. Specifically, we show that for a simple scheduling problem and for low degree spanning trees, when guided by a heuristic version of ALDrIFT called TopIFT, an LLM (GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2018)) can adapt its generative distribution to favor solutions with low d⁡(s)d(s) values while still respecting its prior, hence qualitatively demonstrating the “mass covering” type behavior required for coarse learnability.

While our formal guarantees do not yet apply to inference-time alignment directly (and likely require relaxed formulations), our aim is to introduce an MBO framework that makes the behavior of expressive and potentially mis-specified models more amenable to analysis. By identifying coverage as a key driver of convergence, we provide a possible theoretical lens for reasoning about how generative models could support combinatorial optimization under appropriate coverage conditions.

Summary of Contributions. We summarize our primary contributions as follows:

  • •

    Conceptual Framework: We introduce coarse learnability (Assumption 2) as a sufficient coverage-style condition to establish finite-sample guarantees for iterative Model-Based Optimization (MBO) using expressive approximate learners.

  • •

    MBO Algorithm: We propose ALDrIFT (Section 3.2), an MBO algorithm that pairs iterative learning of generative models with a principled sampling correction step (e.g., Metropolis-Hastings) to control the accumulation of approximation errors.

  • •

    General Theoretical Guarantee: We prove that under Assumption 2, ALDrIFT achieves polynomial finite-sample convergence to the target pTp_{T} (Theorem 1).

  • •

    Unconditional Instantiation: To ground our framework, we analyze ALDrIFT in the canonical setting of ε\varepsilon-globally optimizing non-convex objectives bounded by a quadratic envelope in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} in Section 5. By employing an optimistic Gaussian proposal, we show that coarse learnability holds in this setting and obtain a sample complexity of 𝒪~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(\log 1/\varepsilon).

  • •

    Supporting Evidence: Finally, we provide proof-of-concept theoretical and qualitative empirical evidence (Sections 6 and 9) demonstrating respectively that certain simple generative models satisfy coarse learnability and that even primitive LLMs can exhibit the mass-covering behavior required by our theoretical framework on combinatorial tasks.

1.2 Related Work

Our work sits at the intersection of several active research areas, including zeroth-order optimization, statistical learning theory, sequential MCMC, and non-convex optimization. We present the most pertinent related work here, and defer related work on non-convex optimization methods to Section 5.4.

Model-Based Optimization and MRAS.

Our approach is formally an instance of the model reference adaptive search (MRAS) framework (Hu et al., 2007), which generalizes the cross-entropy method (Rubinstein, 1999). MRAS operates by using a parametric model to approximate a sequence of ideal target distributions that increasingly concentrate on the optimum. In each epoch, it generates samples from the current parametric model, selects the high-performing “elite” samples, and updates the model parameters to fit this elite set. While MRAS is proven to converge in the limit to the globally optimal solution when the parametric distributions are from an exponential family, it lacks sample complexity bounds, both for simple parametric families as well as for expressive approximate learners, which is the focus of our paper. We present this connection in more detail in Section A.2.

Our work also bears similarity to reinforcement learning algorithms like reward-weighted regression (Peters and Schaal, 2007) and relative entropy policy search (Peters et al., 2010). These methods typically view the optimization as an Expectation-Maximization (EM) problem. Our framework differs by explicitly acknowledging that the ‘M-step’ (learning the generative model) may be imperfect (coarse). Our main contribution is modeling this coarseness and developing polynomial sample complexity bounds by correcting for these imperfections via Metropolis–Hastings.

Sequential Monte-Carlo Sampling.

The annealing structure of ALDrIFT, progressing through a sequence of tempered distributions pτ​(s)∝ℒ⁡(s)​e−τ​d​(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)e^{-\tau d(s)} with Metropolis–Hastings corrections at each step, shares a foundational skeleton with Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS; (Neal, 1998)) and Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC; (Del Moral et al., 2006; Andrieu et al., 2010)). However, these methods maintain a discrete empirical measure over particles, while ALDrIFT introduces a parametric projection step: it fits a generative model to the particles at each temperature, which is then used as the proposal for the next step. In effect, this replaces the variance associated with importance weights and particle degeneracy with approximation bias, as the fitted model ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} may not faithfully cover the target pτp_{\tau}. While related ideas appear in adaptive and amortized sampling methods, this projection step introduces a distinct source of error not present in classical particle-based schemes, which we address via the coarse learnability assumption.

Population Monte Carlo (PMC; Cappé et al. (2004)) shares a similar overall structure to ALDrIFT. It iteratively fits a parametric proposal to a particle population; however, in our setting, the variance in weights can explode. ALDrIFT circumvents this by defining a sequence of intermediate targets and utilizing Metropolis-Hastings to draw unweighted samples from them. Consequently, our contribution is to present sufficient conditions under which such unweighted sampling has polynomial complexity.

Furthermore, while recent work on amortized MCMC via transport maps similarly focuses on “learning to propose” to improve acceptance rates (Parno and Marzouk, 2018; Brofos et al., 2022; Hoffman et al., 2019), we introduce a finite-sample coverage assumption (Assumption 2) rather than relying on accuracy of the learned transport map to improve sampling efficiency.

Learnability and Coverage.

In contrast to classical statistical learning theory concepts such as probably approximately correct (PAC) learning (Valiant, 1984), our paper introduces the notion of coarse learnability (Assumption 2). This concept is loosely related to the coverage condition studied in reinforcement learning (Szepesvári and Munos, 2005; Xie et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2025) and recent work on inference-time alignment (Huang et al., 2025). In those settings, bounded coverage is typically a static assumption on the data distribution or behavior policy, ensuring sufficient overlap with the optimal policy to permit valid estimation. Coarse learnability plays a similar structural role, but differs by treating coverage as a statistical outcome of the model fitting. It posits that given polynomial samples from a target, the generative model learns to cover that target (within polynomial factors), effectively regenerating the required coverage dynamically at each iteration.

Bandit Convex Optimization.

Our problem involves optimizing an objective d⁡(s)d(s) where only function evaluations are available. This is related to bandit convex optimization (BCO) (Flaxman et al., 2005), which provides regret bounds for online convex minimization with only noisy function evaluations. Conceptually, if the LLM’s probability function ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) were log-concave and the algorithmic cost d⁡(s)d(s) convex, the target distribution pτ​(s)∝ℒ⁡(s)​e−τ​d​(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)e^{-\tau d(s)} would be log-concave, making it amenable to BCO techniques. Our framework extends this to the general scenario where the prior ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) need not be log-concave, and the function d⁡(s)d(s) need not be convex. We therefore need a somewhat weaker learnability condition that is applicable to these situations.

Bayesian Methods.

Coarse learnability is conceptually related to posterior-contraction results in Bayesian nonparametrics (Ghosal and van der Vaart, 2017; van der Vaart and van Zanten, 2008), which characterize how a Bayesian posterior concentrates around the true distribution with increasing data. Unlike those asymptotic consistency results, our assumption is a finite-sample condition ensuring that a learned generative model maintains sufficient mass on high-value regions during iterative optimization. Finally, our work bears superficial similarity to the use of Bayesian posteriors in guiding exploration (Srinivas et al., 2010; Russo and Van Roy, 2014). However, in those settings the posterior merely quantifies uncertainty and could be replaced by frequentist confidence bounds such as UCB. In contrast, in our framework the generative model is an integral component of the optimization process itself, progressively refining its distribution toward the optimal solution.

2 Optimization Framework with a Generative Model

We consider the problem of minimizing a global objective function d:S→ℜd:S\to\Re, where SS is the solution space.11 1 In practice, SS is conditioned on the prompt string xx, which encodes the local and global constraints of the problem instance; we omit xx from the subsequent discussion. As is standard in MCMC literature, we assume w.l.o.g. that d⁡(s)∈[0,D]d(s)\in[0,D] for all s∈Ss\in S. We assume only zeroth-order oracle access to d⁡(s)d(s): we can evaluate d⁡(s)d(s) for any s∈Ss\in S, but do not have access to its gradients. In our canonical applications (e.g., Section 9), d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) can typically be computed efficiently by an algorithm. In addition, we assume access to a prior distribution ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s). This prior ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) can be modeled by a generative distribution, such as that provided by parametrized or generative models.

Our goal is to identify solutions ss that attain low values of d⁡(s)d(s) while also having high probability under ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s). This objective can be formulated as sampling from, or finding the modes of, the target distribution:

pT(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−T⋅d(s),p_{T}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-T\cdot d(s)},

where T>0T>0 is a ‘temperature’ parameter that controls how sharply pT​(s)p_{T}(s) concentrates on solutions ss that minimize d⁡(s)d(s) among those with significant probability mass under ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s).

This sampling problem is particularly interesting when the generative model ℒ\mathcal{L} is very unlikely to generate solutions with small d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot), and when a random solution ss with low d⁡(s)d(s) is also very unlikely to have relatively high probability under ℒ\mathcal{L} compared to a carefully chosen ss. We assume that given samples from any distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, we can use these samples to learn a distribution that is close to 𝒟\mathcal{D}, for instance, via parameter-fitting. We will make the learning assumption more precise later, and this will be one of our key contributions.

In the sequel, we use s∼ℒs\sim\mathcal{L} to denote that the sample ss is generated by a model ℒ\mathcal{L}. For distributions P,QP,Q, let dtv​(P,Q)d_{\mathrm{tv}}(P,Q) denote the total variation distance between them.

3 ALDrIFT: An Algorithm with Provable Guarantees

We now develop our algorithm ALDrIFT for solving the sampling problem above, with provable guarantees. Before presenting the algorithm, we first discuss a natural heuristic, TopIFT, which highlights key technical challenges in obtaining formal bounds and thereby motivates both our algorithm and the assumptions underlying it.

3.1 A Simple Heuristic: TopIFT

To build intuition for why our sampling problem is non-trivial, we begin with a natural heuristic, TopIFT, which iteratively refines the model by sampling from the current distribution, selecting the lowest-cost samples, and fitting a model to this elite set. Although effective empirically, TopIFT highlights the challenges that motivate the principled algorithm, ALDrIFT (Section 3.2).

At iteration rr, the heuristic draws m⋅Mm\cdot M samples from the current model ℒr−1\mathcal{L}_{r-1}, evaluates the zeroth-order cost d⁡(s)d(s) for each sample, selects the best mm samples, and learns ℒr−1\mathcal{L}_{r-1} using this set to obtain ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r}. The cost function d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) thus guides the refinement of the model in conjunction with the prior.

The heuristic in Section 3.1 is closely related to the cross-entropy (CE) method (Rubinstein, 1999), where an “elite” set of high-performing samples is repeatedly used to update a parametric model via MLE. In our setting, the generative model plays the role of the parametric family, and model-fitting corresponds to the MLE update. However, CE-style updates are difficult to analyze, since the hard-min elite-selection step can induce mode collapse and eliminate coverage of important regions.

These difficulties manifest directly in TopIFT: Its hard-min selection step is analytically brittle, and repeated model-fitting without explicit control over density ratios can progressively erode probability mass on rare but critical regions. ALDrIFT resolves these issues by replacing hard-min with a controlled annealing schedule and by introducing Metropolis–Hastings corrections (Section 3.2), ensuring that samples at each iteration follow the correct intermediate target distribution; this prevents coverage errors from compounding across iterations. We present the connection between ALDrIFT and TopIFT in more detail in Section A.1, and empirically demonstrate the need for iterated distribution correction in Section 7.

To implement the Metropolis–Hastings correction and hence show our theoretical results, we require the following assumption. This assumption holds whenever the generative model admits tractable likelihood evaluation, including many autoregressive sequence models and open weight models.

Assumption 1.

For any s∈Ss\in S, the probability value ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) is available. This must hold not only for the initial model but also for any intermediate models obtained.

3.2 ALDrIFT Algorithm

Our final algorithm, ALDrIFT, is presented in Section 3.2. The input to ALDrIFT is the number of samples (m=poly⁡(T,D)m=\mathrm{poly}(T,D)), and the parameter TT. We set M=m2M=m^{2}. Recall that D=maxs∈S⁡d⁡(s)D=\max_{s\in S}d(s).

In this algorithm, we intend the model ℒτ​(s)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(s) to be an approximation to pτ(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−τ⋅d(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-\tau\cdot d(s)}, where the temperature parameter τ\tau will gradually increase from 00 to TT. The main difference between ALDrIFT and TopIFT is that the probability of retaining a sample is adjusted based on the target distribution pτp_{\tau}. This adjustment is an interesting application of the Metropolis–Hastings algorithm (Metropolis et al., 1953), which runs the IMH chain for MM steps until mixing. We require Assumption 1 for both ℒ\mathcal{L} and the intermediate learned models ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau}, in particular to enable MCMC sampling from pτp_{\tau} given a model for pτ​-p_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}. As discussed in Section 4, this prevents errors in model learning from accumulating across iterations.

Remarks. In Section 3.2, we use a single complexity parameter mm to control multiple aspects of the algorithm for simplicity of analysis. As stated in Assumption 2, mm primarily serves as a learnability parameter, i.e., the number of samples required. We also use mm to determine both the number of Metropolis–Hastings iterations (running the step mm times) and the length of each iteration (M=m2M=m^{2}). This ensures that the computational effort per simulated annealing step scales polynomially with the learnability parameter. Further, in certain cases like the setting in Sections 5 and 7, the dependence of the run-time on DD can be removed via a geometric annealing schedule. We also note that the model-fitting step is efficient in practice if we use the parameters of ℒτ−\mathcal{L}_{\tau-} as an efficient starting point to learn ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau}, preventing the need to learn from scratch in each iteration. Finally, Section 3.2 is an instance of Model Reference Adaptive Search (MRAS) (Hu et al., 2007), which generalizes the cross-entropy method (Rubinstein, 1999). We present this connection in Section A.2.

4 Coarse Learnability and Sample Complexity of ALDrIFT

We will analyze the sample complexity of ALDrIFT in Section 4. To do this, we need an assumption on the learning agent. In Section 4, we propose the novel “coarse learnability” assumption, which essentially says that if we can approximately generate samples from pτp_{\tau}, then we can coarsely learn a model ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} for it using the samples. Coarse learnability asks only that model fitting produce a proposal with tails heavy enough to cover the target up to polynomial density ratios (in the number of samples used) on all but exponentially rare target mass.

For two distributions pp and LL on the same support SS, we define the coverage of LL with respect to pp at a point s∈Ss\in S as covp,L​(s)=p⁡(s)L⁡(s).\mathrm{cov}_{p,L}(s)\;=\;\frac{p(s)}{L(s)}. This notion, similar to analogous notions in reinforcement learning and inference-time alignment (e.g., (Xie et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025)), quantifies how well the proposal distribution LL “covers” the probability mass of the target pp: large values indicate under-coverage, while small values indicate over-coverage.

Assumption 2 (Coarse Learnability).

For each temperature τ∈[0,T]\tau\in[0,T], let pτ​(s)∝ℒ0​(s)⋅e−τ​d​(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}_{0}(s)\cdot e^{-\tau d(s)} be the target distribution and ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} the model obtained after fitting. We say the model family satisfies coarse learnability if for any large enough K≥poly⁡(D,T)K\geq\mathrm{poly}(D,T) and any error ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) and confidence δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1), there is a sample size m=poly⁡(K/δ,ln⁡1/ε)m=\mathrm{poly}(K/\delta,\ln 1/\varepsilon) such that the following holds:

If ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} is trained using mm samples from a distribution p^\hat{p}, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta (over the training samples), the learned model satisfies:

Prs∼pτ[covpτ,ℒτ(s)>K]≤O(dtv(p^,pτ))+ε.\Pr_{s\sim p_{\tau}}\!\left[\mathrm{cov}_{p_{\tau},\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}(s)>K\right]\leq O\left(d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})\right)+\varepsilon. (1)

The key distinction between Assumption 2 and standard density estimation or PAC learning (Valiant, 1984) lies in the error regime. Standard guarantees typically yield error rates polynomial in the sample size (ε≈poly​(1/m)\varepsilon\approx\text{poly}(1/m)). In contrast, our sample complexity mm scales with ln⁡(1/ε)\ln(1/\varepsilon), which means polynomial samples yield exponentially small error probabilities (ε≈e−m\varepsilon\approx e^{-m}), albeit for a coarse coverage guarantee. This stronger tail bound is needed for the following reason. Since we assumed the global optimum could have exponentially small probability under the initial prior, a learner with only polynomial error guarantees could validly assign vanishing probability to the optimal region. The exponential tail bound ensures that the intermediate models preserve coverage of these rare regions throughout the annealing schedule.

To build intuition, we consider the following simplification. Assume p^=pτ\hat{p}=p_{\tau}. For given KK, set ε=e−K\varepsilon=e^{-K} and δ=1/K\delta=1/K. Assumption 2 now implies K=mβK=m^{\beta} for some constant β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1). If we re-parametrize in terms of mm, we have ε=e−mβ\varepsilon=e^{-m^{\beta}}. In this regime, K≤mK\leq m, so that we can use mm instead of KK in Eq. 1, which yields Pr[covpτ,ℒτ(s)>m]≤ε=e−mβ.\Pr\left[\mathrm{cov}_{p_{\tau},\mathcal{L}_{\tau}}(s)>m\right]\leq\varepsilon=e^{-m^{\beta}}. Then, Assumption 2 simplifies to the following property for general parametric models and targets:

Assumption 2, special case. A model ℒ\mathcal{L} coarsely learns a parametric distribution pp if for sufficiently large sample size mm that depends polynomially on the parameters of the distribution, w.p. 1−1/mβ1-1/m^{\beta}, the model ℒm\mathcal{L}^{m} trained on mm samples from pp satisfies Pr[covp,ℒm(s)>m]≤e−mβ\Pr\left[\text{cov}_{p,\mathcal{L}^{m}}(s)>m\right]\leq e^{-m^{\beta}}, where β>0\beta>0 is a small constant.

Coarse learnability guarantees polynomial coverage of the target density, except on an atypical set of exponentially small measure. Unlike density estimation guarantees that require the total variation distance to vanish, this condition allows for persistent approximation errors (model mis-specification; see Section 6.1). This extends coverage-based analyses (Huang et al., 2025) to the iterative setting, where as long as the coverage remains polynomially bounded, the M-H correction can recover the exact target distribution, bridging regimes where the initial coverage gap is exponentially large via intermediate polynomial steps. While this appears to be a strong assumption, such intuition is implicit in classical MBO (Rubinstein, 1999; Hu et al., 2007), and is fundamentally linked to statistical estimators that prioritize heavy tails (e.g., over-smoothed KDE). In Section 7, we empirically demonstrate a non-convex optimization setting where an inflated proposal with distribution correction allow for the global convergence of ALDrIFT when sample budgets are small. In Section 6, we provide evidence supporting the plausibility of Assumption 2 for well-known generative distributions.

Our main analytical result analyzes the sample complexity of ALDrIFT under coarse learnability.

Theorem 1 (Proved in Section 4.1).

Under Assumption 2, for sufficiently large m=poly​(T,D)m=\mbox{poly}(T,D) the sample complexity of ALDrIFT is O⁡(m​M​T​D)=poly⁡(T,D)O(mMTD)=\mathrm{poly}(T,D), and with high probability, the sampling distribution p^\hat{p} of STS_{T} satisfies22 2 Since pτp_{\tau} is only coarsely learnable via ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau}, we need to consider the dtvd_{\mathrm{tv}} with respect to the sampling distribution SτS_{\tau}, which corrects this coarse learning error via the Metropolis–Hastings procedure. dtv​(p^,pT)=O⁡(e−mα)d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{T})=O\left(e^{-m^{\alpha}}\right), where α>0\alpha>0 is a constant.

4.1 Proof of Theorem 1

Our proof focuses on a particular iteration τ>0\tau>0. We consider the inner loops of ALDrIFT, where we generate the set of samples SτS_{\tau} using Metropolis-Hastings. Let Wτ−={s∣pτ−​(s)≤m⋅ℒτ−​(s)}W_{\tau^{-}}=\{s\mid p_{\tau^{-}}(s)\leq m\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\tau^{-}}(s)\} be the “typical set” where the proposal covers the previous target, and let η=Prpτ−⁡[Wτ−c]\eta=\Pr_{p_{\tau^{-}}}[W_{\tau^{-}}^{c}] be the mass of the atypical set.

Lemma 2.

At step τ\tau, let ℰ\mathcal{E} be the event that the Metropolis-Hastings chain in ALDrIFT encounters a state s∈Wτ−cs\in W_{\tau^{-}}^{c} at any step during the generation of the mm samples in SτS_{\tau}. With probability at least 1−m2​η1-m^{2}\eta, the event ℰ\mathcal{E} does not occur. Conditioned on ¬ℰ\neg\mathcal{E}, the distribution p^\hat{p} of any sample generated by the chain satisfies:

dtv(p^,pτ)≤e⋅η+e−m/e.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})\leq e\cdot\eta+e^{-m/e}. (2)
Proof.

First, since pτ−​(s)>m⋅ℒτ−​(s)p_{\tau^{-}}(s)>m\cdot\mathcal{L}_{\tau^{-}}(s) for all s∈Wτ​-cs\in W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c}, we have

Prs∼ℒτ​-[s∈Wτ​-c]≤1mPrpτ​-[Wτ​-c]=ηm.\Pr_{s\sim\mathcal{L}_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}}[s\in W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c}]\leq\frac{1}{m}\Pr_{p_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}}[W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c}]=\frac{\eta}{m}.

The algorithm takes M=m2M=m^{2} steps per sample, for a total of mm samples. By a union bound over all these steps, the probability that a state in Wτ​-cW_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c} is ever proposed is at most m3⋅(η/m)=m2​ηm^{3}\cdot(\eta/m)=m^{2}\eta. This establishes the probability bound for event ℰ\mathcal{E}.

Conditioned on ¬ℰ\neg\mathcal{E}, the chain operates entirely within Wτ​-W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}. Since pτ(s)∝pτ​-(s)e−d(s)/Dp_{\tau}(s)\propto p_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}(s)e^{-d(s)/D} and since d⁡(s)∈[0,D]d(s)\in[0,D] for all ss, this means pτ​(s)≤e⋅pτ−​(s)p_{\tau}(s)\leq e\cdot p_{\tau^{-}}(s). Thus, for any s∈Wτ​-s\in W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}, the density ratio with respect to the new target is bounded:

pτ​(s)ℒτ​-​(s)≤e⋅pτ​-​(s)ℒτ​-​(s)≤e⋅m.\frac{p_{\tau}(s)}{\mathcal{L}_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}(s)}\leq e\cdot\frac{p_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}(s)}{\mathcal{L}_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}(s)}\leq e\cdot m.

The sampling procedure is therefore equivalent to an independent Metropolis–Hastings (IMH) chain restricted to Wτ​-W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}} with density ratio bounded by e​mem. By the uniform ergodicity of IMH (Mengersen and Tweedie, 1996; Tierney, 1994), the variation distance to the restricted target pτ′∝pτ|Wτ−p^{\prime}_{\tau}\propto p_{\tau}|_{W_{\tau^{-}}} after M=m2M=m^{2} steps is:

dtv(p^,pτ′)≤(1−1e​m)M≤e−m/e.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p^{\prime}_{\tau})\leq\left(1-\frac{1}{em}\right)^{M}\leq e^{-m/e}.

We finally bound the distance to the true target pτp_{\tau}. The error introduced by restricting the target to Wτ​-W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}} is bounded by the mass of the excluded set under pτp_{\tau}:

dtv​(pτ′,pτ)=pτ​(Wτ​-c)≤e⋅pτ​-​(Wτ​-c)=e⋅η.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(p^{\prime}_{\tau},p_{\tau})=p_{\tau}(W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c})\leq e\cdot p_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}(W_{\tau{\scalebox{0.8}[0.8]{-}}}^{c})=e\cdot\eta.

By the triangle inequality:

dtv(p^,pτ)≤dtv(p^,pτ′)+dtv(pτ′,pτ)≤e−m/e+e⋅η.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})\leq d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p^{\prime}_{\tau})+d_{\mathrm{tv}}(p^{\prime}_{\tau},p_{\tau})\leq e^{-m/e}+e\cdot\eta.

This completes the proof. ∎

Using the above lemma, we now complete the proof of Theorem 1.

Proof of Theorem 1.

As in the text following Assumption 2, we set ε=exp⁡(−K)\varepsilon=\exp(-K) and δ=1/K\delta=1/K, so that K=mβK=m^{\beta} for constant β>0\beta>0. We now choose mm large enough that mβ=ω⁡(T​D)m^{\beta}=\omega(TD), and note that m≥Km\geq K.

We prove by induction that if the algorithm succeeds (does not hit atypical sets), then for all τ\tau, dtv​(p^,pτ)=O⁡(e−mα)d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})=O(e^{-m^{\alpha}}) for some constant α∈(0,β)\alpha\in(0,\beta). For the base case, note that dtv​(p^,p0)=0d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{0})=0 since we begin with the model ℒ0=ℒ\mathcal{L}_{0}=\mathcal{L}. For the inductive step, assume dtv​(p^,pτ−)≤εprevd_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau^{-}})\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{prev}}. By Assumption 2, the learned model ℒτ−\mathcal{L}_{\tau^{-}} has an atypical set mass η≤O⁡(εprev)+e−mβ\eta\leq O(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{prev}})+e^{-m^{\beta}}. Applying Lemma 2, the error at the next step is:

dtv(p^,pτ)≤e⋅(O(εprev)+e−mβ)+e−m/e.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})\leq e\cdot\left(O\left(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{prev}}\right)+e^{-m^{\beta}}\right)+e^{-m/e}.

Unrolling this recurrence over T⋅DT\cdot D steps results in an error growth of ϕT​D\phi^{TD} for some constant ϕ>1\phi>1. Thus:

dtv​(p^,pT)=O⁡(ϕT​D⋅e−mβ)=eO⁡(T​D)−mβ.d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{T})=O\left(\phi^{TD}\cdot e^{-m^{\beta}}\right)=e^{O(TD)-m^{\beta}}.

Assuming mβ=ω⁡(T​D)m^{\beta}=\omega(TD), we have dtv​(p^,pT)=O⁡(e−mα)d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{T})=O(e^{-m^{\alpha}}). This completes the induction.

The algorithm fails at any step τ\tau if (a) learning fails (probability δ\delta) or (b) sampling hits WcW^{c} (probability m2⋅ηm^{2}\cdot\eta). The above derivation yields η=O⁡(e−mα)\eta=O(e^{-m^{\alpha}}), so that we have m2​η=o⁡(m−β)m^{2}\eta=o\left(m^{-\beta}\right). Further, δ=1/K=m−β\delta=1/K=m^{-\beta}. By a union bound over T⋅DT\cdot D steps, total failure probability is O⁡(T⋅D⋅m−β)=o⁡(1)O(T\cdot D\cdot m^{-\beta})=o(1) since we assume mβ=ω⁡(T​D)m^{\beta}=\omega(TD).

Finally, at given any τ\tau, the total number of samples is O⁡(m3)=poly⁡(T,D)O(m^{3})=\mathrm{poly}(T,D). This completes the proof of Theorem 1. ∎

5 Sample Complexity of ALDrIFT for Bounded Non-Convex Optimization

Classical zeroth-order global optimization in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} often relies on local Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods (Kalai and Vempala, 2006). While these methods achieve polynomial time complexity on strictly log-concave target distributions, they can require exponential time to mix on non-convex landscapes due to local energy barriers (Holley and Stroock, 1987; Hajek, 1988). We prove that Model-Based Optimization (MBO) overcomes this limitation, and achieves logarithmic sample complexity in the precision parameter, hence providing a finite-sample analog to the asymptotic convergence results for MRAS.

By leveraging a modification of ALDrIFT with an inflated proposal distribution ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau}, we show that it can efficiently (globally) optimize non-convex functions that are bounded by a quadratic envelope. In particular, we show that Assumption 2 holds at all intermediate steps with a bound KK that is independent of the temperature parameter τ\tau, guaranteeing sample complexity O~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon) to achieve error ε\varepsilon in the global optimum, matching the bounds of space partitioning methods (Munos, 2011; Bubeck et al., 2011) for this setting (under some caveats that we mention in Section 5.4). The O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) notation hides constants that depend on n,Kn,K, and log⁡1δ\log\frac{1}{\delta}.

Recall that in Section 7, we presented an empirical demonstration of the need for an inflated proposal distribution (with sample correction) in ensuring the convergence of ALDrIFT with limited sample budgets, comparing it to TopIFT that uses the empirical variance and samples without distribution correction, and gets trapped in local optima.

5.1 Optimization Setting and Algorithm

The domain is ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. Assume the generative prior is a Gaussian ℒ0​(x)∝exp⁡(−U⁡(x))\mathcal{L}_{0}(x)\propto\exp(-U(x)), where U⁡(x)=μ02​‖x−x0‖2U(x)=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2}\|x-x_{0}\|^{2} for some μ0>0\mu_{0}>0.

Assume the objective d⁡(x)d(x) has a unique global minimum at x∗x^{*}. We assume d⁡(x)d(x) is bounded by a quadratic envelope around its true optimum: there exist constants μd,Ld>0\mu_{d},L_{d}>0 such that for all x∈ℝnx\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

μd2​‖x−x∗‖2≤d⁡(x)−d⁡(x∗)≤Ld2​‖x−x∗‖2.\displaystyle\frac{\mu_{d}}{2}\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}\leq d(x)-d(x^{*})\leq\frac{L_{d}}{2}\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}.

Note that d⁡(x)d(x) is not assumed to be convex and may contain arbitrary local non-convexities within these bounds. This model is well-studied in non-convex optimization; see for instance (Munos, 2011; Bubeck et al., 2011).

We now run ALDrIFT for NN steps as described in Section 5.3. There are changes needed to the algorithm to handle the lack of an upper bound on d⁡(x)d(x), and to make the sampling process exact, that we detail there. We also detail the parameter settings there, and re-do the proof of sample complexity.

When the temperature parameter is τ\tau, the target distribution is pτ​(x)∝exp⁡(−fτ​(x))p_{\tau}(x)\propto\exp(-f_{\tau}(x)), where fτ​(x)=U⁡(x)+τ​d​(x)f_{\tau}(x)=U(x)+\tau d(x). The algorithm draws mm samples from pτp_{\tau} (where the parameter mm will be chosen later), computes the empirical mean ω^τ\hat{\omega}_{\tau}, and fits the proposal distribution (or generative model) ℒτ​(x)=𝒩⁡(ω^τ,2μτ​In)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x)=\mathcal{N}(\hat{\omega}_{\tau},\frac{2}{\mu_{\tau}}I_{n}), where μτ=μ0+τ​μd\mu_{\tau}=\mu_{0}+\tau\mu_{d}. We assume the sampling is exactly from pτp_{\tau}, and we justify this in Section 5.3. It is also crucial for our proof of Theorem 3 below that the distribution has larger variance than desired and is set based on the convex envelope parameters μd,Ld\mu_{d},L_{d}, hence deviating from standard MBO that uses the sample variance directly.

5.2 Verifying Coarse Learnability

We now show that Assumption 2 holds at all intermediate steps of the algorithm, for the proposal distribution ℒτ​(x)=𝒩⁡(ω^τ,2μτ​In)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x)=\mathcal{N}(\hat{\omega}_{\tau},\frac{2}{\mu_{\tau}}I_{n}). Note that in this setting, Assumption 2 is not an assumption; we show that it holds because of our choice of the model ℒτ​(x)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x).

To simplify presentation, we define the following global geometric constants:

  • •

    The proxy condition number: κmax=max⁡(2,Ldμd)\kappa_{\max}=\max\left(2,\frac{L_{d}}{\mu_{d}}\right).

  • •

    The initial shift penalty: Eshift=μ02​‖x0−x∗‖2E_{\text{shift}}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2}\|x_{0}-x^{*}\|^{2}.

  • •

    The inflation factor: B=κmaxn/2​exp⁡(Eshift)B=\kappa_{\max}^{n/2}\exp(E_{\text{shift}}).

We will further assume in the rest of the section that d⁡(x∗)=0d(x^{*})=0, so that d⁡(x)≥0d(x)\geq 0 for all xx. This is w.l.o.g., since the normalized density pτp_{\tau} remains unchanged if we replace d⁡(x)d(x) with d~​(x)=d⁡(x)−d⁡(x∗)\tilde{d}(x)=d(x)-d(x^{*}), so that the algorithm’s execution remains identical.

Theorem 3 (Coarse Learnability of pτp_{\tau}).

Given the setting and algorithm defined above, if the per-step sample size satisfies m≥C⁡(n2​ln⁡κmax+Eshift)​(n+ln⁡Nδ)m\geq C\left(\frac{n}{2}\ln\kappa_{\max}+E_{\text{shift}}\right)\left(n+\ln\frac{N}{\delta}\right) for constant C>0C>0, then for any temperature τ\tau, the model ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} globally satisfies the following condition33 3 This condition is slightly different from how Assumption 2 is phrased, but suffices for the sample complexity proof in Section 5.3. with probability at least 1−δ/(2​N)1-\delta/(2N):

supx∈ℝnpτ​(x)ℒτ​(x)≤2n/2⋅B5⋅exp⁡(1+2​n):=K.\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}\frac{p_{\tau}(x)}{\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x)}\leq 2^{n/2}\cdot B^{5}\cdot\exp\left(1+2n\right):=K.
Remarks.

Theorem 3 can be viewed as a special case of the Coarse Learnability assumption (Assumption 2). Because Theorem 3 establishes a global supremum bound on the density ratio, we have Pr[ratio>K]=0\Pr[\text{ratio}>K]=0. Furthermore, because we utilize Rejection Sampling (Section 5.3), the empirical samples are drawn perfectly from the target, meaning dtv​(p^,pτ)=0d_{\mathrm{tv}}(\hat{p},p_{\tau})=0. Consequently, the inequality in Assumption 2 is satisfied for any ε>0\varepsilon>0. Further, the sample complexity is m=poly​(ln⁡K,ln⁡1/δ)m=\mbox{poly}\left(\ln K,\ln 1/\delta\right), which is stronger than the bound in Assumption 2, assuming KK is a large enough function of the problem parameters (but independent of TT). Theorem 3 suffices for the specialized analysis of ALDrIFT that we perform in Section 5.3.

Note that KK (and consequently the algorithm’s sample complexity) does not grow with τ\tau. This non-asymptotically captures the limiting behavior predicted by Laplace’s method (Wong, 2001) and the Bernstein-von Mises theorem (van der Vaart, 1998) in Bayesian inference: as the τ\tau-scaled regularizer overwhelms the prior, the prior collapses into a constant spatial penalty evaluated at the optimum. However, while those classical theorems are valid only as τ→∞\tau\to\infty, our quadratic envelope technique provides an upper bound for any finite τ≥0\tau\geq 0.

The rest of this subsection is devoted to proving this theorem.

Upper Bounding pτp_{\tau}.

We now show a sequence of lemmas that will bound the density ratio. We start with pτp_{\tau}, and bound it via standard methods.

Lemma 4 (Target Envelope).

The target distribution pτ​(x)p_{\tau}(x) is globally upper-bounded by a scaled Gaussian envelope:

pτ​(x)≤B⋅(μτ2​π)n/2​exp⁡(−μτ2​‖x−x¯τ‖2)\displaystyle p_{\tau}(x)\leq B\cdot\left(\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2}\|x-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\right)

where x¯τ=μ0​x0+τ​μd​x∗μτ\bar{x}_{\tau}=\frac{\mu_{0}x_{0}+\tau\mu_{d}x^{*}}{\mu_{\tau}}.

Proof.

Let the target probability distribution be defined as pτ​(x)=1Zτ​exp⁡(−fτ​(x))p_{\tau}(x)=\frac{1}{Z_{\tau}}\exp(-f_{\tau}(x)), where fτ​(x)=μ02​‖x−x0‖2+τ​d​(x)f_{\tau}(x)=\frac{\mu_{0}}{2}\|x-x_{0}\|^{2}+\tau d(x) and Zτ=∫ℝnexp⁡(−fτ​(x))​𝑑xZ_{\tau}=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\exp(-f_{\tau}(x))dx is the normalizing constant.

By assumption, d⁡(x)d(x) is bounded by quadratics: μd2​‖x−x∗‖2≤d⁡(x)≤Ld2​‖x−x∗‖2\frac{\mu_{d}}{2}\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}\leq d(x)\leq\frac{L_{d}}{2}\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}. We can therefore sandwich fτ​(x)f_{\tau}(x) between a lower bounding quadratic fτ,low​(x)f_{\tau,\text{low}}(x) and an upper bounding quadratic fτ,up​(x)f_{\tau,\text{up}}(x):

Sub-Gaussian Upper Bound.

Let q⁡(x)=𝒩⁡(x¯τ,1μτ​In)q(x)=\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}_{\tau},\frac{1}{\mu_{\tau}}I_{n}). From Lemma 4, we have: pτ​(x)≤B⋅q⁡(x)p_{\tau}(x)\leq B\cdot q(x). We now have the following lemmas using this inequality, which will help us bound the density ratio. We provide the proof of the lemma below for completeness.

Lemma 6.

Let ω~τ=𝔼pτ​[x]\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}=\mathbb{E}_{p_{\tau}}[x] be the true expectation. Then,

μτ​‖ω~τ−x¯τ‖2≤(n+2​ln⁡B)2≤2​n+4​ln⁡B.\mu_{\tau}\|\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq\left(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{2\ln B}\right)^{2}\leq 2n+4\ln B.
Proof.

By Jensen’s inequality, ‖ω~τ−x¯τ‖2≤𝔼pτ​[‖x−x¯τ‖2]\|\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq\mathbb{E}_{p_{\tau}}[\|x-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}]. Let z=μτ​(x−x¯τ)z=\sqrt{\mu_{\tau}}(x-\bar{x}_{\tau}). Under the proposal distribution qq, z∼𝒩⁡(0,In)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{n}), which we denote by ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z). Under the target distribution, zz follows some density p⁡(z)p(z). Since zz and xx are linearly related, we have p⁡(z)≤B​ϕ​(z)p(z)\leq B\phi(z). We seek to bound 𝔼p​[‖z‖2]\mathbb{E}_{p}[\|z\|^{2}]. Since p⁡(z)≤B​ϕ​(z)p(z)\leq B\phi(z), the Kullback-Leibler divergence is bounded:

DK​L(p∥ϕ)=𝔼p[lnp⁡(z)ϕ⁡(z)]≤𝔼p[lnB]=lnB.D_{KL}(p\|\phi)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[\ln\frac{p(z)}{\phi(z)}\right]\leq\mathbb{E}_{p}[\ln B]=\ln B.

By the Donsker-Varadhan representation Boucheron et al. (2013), for any measurable function f⁡(z)f(z) and any λ>0\lambda>0:

𝔼p[λf(z)]−ln𝔼ϕ[eλ​f​(z)]≤DK​L(p∥ϕ)⟹𝔼p[f(z)]≤1λ(DK​L(p∥ϕ)+ln𝔼ϕ[eλ​f​(z)]).\mathbb{E}_{p}[\lambda f(z)]-\ln\mathbb{E}_{\phi}[e^{\lambda f(z)}]\leq D_{KL}(p\|\phi)\implies\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(z)]\leq\frac{1}{\lambda}\left(D_{KL}(p\|\phi)+\ln\mathbb{E}_{\phi}[e^{\lambda f(z)}]\right).

We choose f⁡(z)=‖z‖2f(z)=\|z\|^{2}. Under ϕ⁡(z)\phi(z), ‖z‖2\|z\|^{2} follows a χn2\chi^{2}_{n} distribution, whose moment generating function is 𝔼ϕ[eλ​‖z‖2]=(1−2λ)−n/2\mathbb{E}_{\phi}[e^{\lambda\|z\|^{2}}]=(1-2\lambda)^{-n/2} for λ<1/2\lambda<1/2. Substituting this and our KL bound yields:

𝔼p​[‖z‖2]≤ln⁡Bλ−n2​λ​ln⁡(1−2​λ).\mathbb{E}_{p}[\|z\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\ln B}{\lambda}-\frac{n}{2\lambda}\ln(1-2\lambda).

Using −ln⁡(1−x)≤x1−x-\ln(1-x)\leq\frac{x}{1-x} for x∈(0,1)x\in(0,1), we set x=2​λx=2\lambda to obtain:

𝔼p​[‖z‖2]≤ln⁡Bλ+n1−2​λ.\mathbb{E}_{p}[\|z\|^{2}]\leq\frac{\ln B}{\lambda}+\frac{n}{1-2\lambda}.

Choosing λ=(2+2​nln⁡B)−1∈(0,1/2)\lambda=\left(2+\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\ln B}}\right)^{-1}\in(0,1/2) yields:

𝔼p​[‖z‖2]≤(n+2​ln⁡B)2≤2​n+4​ln⁡B.\mathbb{E}_{p}[\|z\|^{2}]\leq\left(\sqrt{n}+\sqrt{2\ln B}\right)^{2}\leq 2n+4\ln B.

Replacing zz with μτ​(x−x¯τ)\sqrt{\mu_{\tau}}(x-\bar{x}_{\tau}) concludes the proof. ∎

Before proceeding, we formally define the variance proxy of a sub-Gaussian random variable (Vershynin, 2018). A random variable ZZ with mean μZ\mu_{Z} is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy ν2\nu^{2} if ZZ satisfies the tail bound Pr(|Z−μZ|≥t)≤2exp(−t2/ν2)\Pr(|Z-\mu_{Z}|\geq t)\leq 2\exp(-t^{2}/\nu^{2}) for all t≥0t\geq 0. A random vector X∈ℝnX\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy ν2\nu^{2} if its one-dimensional projections ⟨X−μX,u⟩\langle X-\mu_{X},u\rangle onto any unit vector u∈𝕊n−1u\in\mathbb{S}^{n-1} are sub-Gaussian with variance proxy ν2\nu^{2}. The following lemma is now straightforward (see (Vershynin, 2018)).

Lemma 7.

X∼pτX\sim p_{\tau} is sub-Gaussian with a variance proxy bounded by ν2=O⁡(1+ln⁡Bμτ)\nu^{2}=O\left(\frac{1+\ln B}{\mu_{\tau}}\right).

We will need the following concentration bound; see (Vershynin, 2018) for a proof.

Lemma 8 (Empirical Mean of Sub-Gaussian Vectors).

Let X1,…,XmX_{1},\dots,X_{m} be independent, identically distributed random vectors in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} with mean ω=𝔼⁡[X1]\omega=\mathbb{E}[X_{1}]. Assume each XiX_{i} is sub-Gaussian with variance proxy ν2\nu^{2}. Let ω^=1m​∑i=1mXi\hat{\omega}=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}X_{i} be the empirical mean. Then, there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that for any t>0t>0, with probability at least 1−e−t1-e^{-t}:

‖ω^−ω‖2≤C​ν2m​(n+t).\displaystyle\|\hat{\omega}-\omega\|^{2}\leq\frac{C\nu^{2}}{m}(n+t).
Proof of Theorem 3.

Using these ingredients, we now prove Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

We evaluate the density ratio rτ​(x)=pτ​(x)/ℒτ​(x)r_{\tau}(x)=p_{\tau}(x)/\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x). The proposal generative model is ℒτ​(x)=𝒩⁡(ω^τ,2μτ​In)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x)=\mathcal{N}(\hat{\omega}_{\tau},\frac{2}{\mu_{\tau}}I_{n}) with density (μτ4​π)n/2​exp⁡(−μτ4​‖x−ω^τ‖2)(\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{4\pi})^{n/2}\exp(-\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{4}\|x-\hat{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}). Using the upper bound from Lemma 4 for the numerator:

rτ​(x)≤B​(μτ2​π)n/2​exp⁡(−μτ2​‖x−x¯τ‖2)(μτ4​π)n/2​exp⁡(−μτ4​‖x−ω^τ‖2)=B​2n/2​exp⁡(−μτ2​‖x−x¯τ‖2+μτ4​‖x−ω^τ‖2).\displaystyle r_{\tau}(x)\leq\frac{B\left(\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2\pi}\right)^{n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2}\|x-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\right)}{\left(\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{4\pi}\right)^{n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{4}\|x-\hat{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}\right)}=B2^{n/2}\exp\left(-\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2}\|x-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}+\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{4}\|x-\hat{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}\right).

We apply triangle inequality: ‖x−ω^τ‖2≤2​‖x−x¯τ‖2+2​‖ω^τ−x¯τ‖2\|x-\hat{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq 2\|x-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}+2\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2} to the second term in the exponent. The xx-dependent terms cancel and we have:

rτ​(x)≤2n/2⋅B⋅exp⁡(μτ2​‖ω^τ−x¯τ‖2).\displaystyle r_{\tau}(x)\leq 2^{n/2}\cdot B\cdot\exp\left(\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2}\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\right). (3)

By the triangle inequality, ‖ω^τ−x¯τ‖2≤2​‖ω^τ−ω~τ‖2+2​‖ω~τ−x¯τ‖2\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq 2\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}+2\|\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}. The exponent in the above expression is therefore bounded by μτ​‖ω^τ−ω~τ‖2+μτ​‖ω~τ−x¯τ‖2\mu_{\tau}\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}+\mu_{\tau}\|\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}. From Lemma 6, we have μτ​‖ω~τ−x¯τ‖2≤2​n+4​ln⁡B\mu_{\tau}\|\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq 2n+4\ln B.

To bound μτ​‖ω^τ−ω~τ‖2\mu_{\tau}\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}, note that ω^τ\hat{\omega}_{\tau} is the empirical mean of mm i.i.d. draws from the target distribution pτp_{\tau}, while ω~τ\tilde{\omega}_{\tau} is the true mean. By Lemma 7, these independent draws from pτp_{\tau} are sub-Gaussian random vectors with a variance proxy bounded by:

ν2=Csg​1+ln⁡Bμτ\displaystyle\nu^{2}=C_{\text{sg}}\frac{1+\ln B}{\mu_{\tau}}

for some constant Csg>0C_{\text{sg}}>0. We now apply Lemma 8. Setting the failure probability to e−t=δ2​Ne^{-t}=\frac{\delta}{2N}, which implies t=ln⁡(2​Nδ)t=\ln\left(\frac{2N}{\delta}\right), we obtain with probability at least 1−δ2​N1-\frac{\delta}{2N}:

‖ω^τ−ω~τ‖2\displaystyle\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2} ≤Cm​ν2​(n+ln⁡(2​Nδ))\displaystyle\leq\frac{C}{m}\nu^{2}\left(n+\ln\left(\frac{2N}{\delta}\right)\right)
=Cm​(Csg​1+ln⁡Bμτ)​(n+ln⁡(2​Nδ)).\displaystyle=\frac{C}{m}\left(C_{\text{sg}}\frac{1+\ln B}{\mu_{\tau}}\right)\left(n+\ln\left(\frac{2N}{\delta}\right)\right).

so that

μτ​‖ω^τ−ω~τ‖2≤C⋅Csgm​(1+ln⁡B)​(n+ln⁡(2​Nδ)).\displaystyle\mu_{\tau}\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\tilde{\omega}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq\frac{C\cdot C_{\text{sg}}}{m}(1+\ln B)\left(n+\ln\left(\frac{2N}{\delta}\right)\right).

m≥C′​(1+ln⁡B)​(n+ln⁡(2​Nδ))\displaystyle m\geq C^{\prime}(1+\ln B)\left(n+\ln\left(\frac{2N}{\delta}\right)\right)

where C′=C⋅CsgC^{\prime}=C\cdot C_{\text{sg}}. Therefore with probability at least 1−δ2​N1-\frac{\delta}{2N}, we have μτ2​‖ω^τ−x¯τ‖2≤1+2​n+4​ln⁡B\frac{\mu_{\tau}}{2}\|\hat{\omega}_{\tau}-\bar{x}_{\tau}\|^{2}\leq 1+2n+4\ln B. Substituting this into Eq. 3 yields the bound on KK. ∎

5.3 Implementing ALDrIFT via Geometric Annealing and Rejection Sampling

Given that we have a simple analytic generative model, we make two changes that both simplify ALDrIFT and lead to an exponentially improved sample complexity. Further note that we did not assume an upper bound on d⁡(x)d(x) in this setting, which needs a different approach than Theorem 1.

In the description below, we set the number of generated samples mm for each temperature from the statement of Theorem 3.

Geometric Annealing.

We use a geometric schedule of temperatures τ\tau. In particular, we set τ0=0\tau_{0}=0, τ1=μ0Ld\tau_{1}=\frac{\mu_{0}}{L_{d}}, and τk+1=(1+γ)⋅τk\tau_{k+1}=(1+\gamma)\cdot\tau_{k} for k≥1k\geq 1, where γ=1/n\gamma=1/n. Since τN≥T\tau_{N}\geq T, this implies the number of outer iterations of ALDrIFT (temperature settings) is N=O⁡(n​ln⁡T​Ldμ0)N=O\left(n\ln\frac{TL_{d}}{\mu_{0}}\right). Such a geometric schedule not only improves the dependence on TT exponentially, but is also robust to d⁡(x)d(x) being unbounded.

Rejection Sampling.

In the inner loop, to generate mm samples from pτk+1p_{\tau_{k+1}}, we use rejection sampling instead of Metropolis-Hastings. Although the normalizing constant Zτk+1Z_{\tau_{k+1}} is unknown, we use Z¯τ:=(2​π/μτ)n/2\bar{Z}_{\tau}:=\left(2\pi/\mu_{\tau}\right)^{n/2} and define the sub-normalized density

p^τ​(x):=exp⁡(−fτ​(x))Z¯τ.\hat{p}_{\tau}(x):=\frac{\exp(-f_{\tau}(x))}{\bar{Z}_{\tau}}.

By Corollary 5, Zτ≤Z¯τZ_{\tau}\leq\bar{Z}_{\tau}. At each sampling step, we generate x∼ℒτkx\sim\mathcal{L}_{\tau_{k}} and accept it with probability

Pr⁡[Accept∣x]=1e​K​B​p^τk+1​(x)ℒτk​(x).\Pr[\mbox{Accept}\mid x]=\frac{1}{\sqrt{e}KB}\frac{\hat{p}_{\tau_{k+1}}(x)}{\mathcal{L}_{\tau_{k}}(x)}.

To generate a sample, we run this process for at most ts=10​K​B2​ln⁡2​N​mδt_{s}=10KB^{2}\ln\frac{2Nm}{\delta} steps, declaring failure if a sample is not generated. We generate mm samples and use them to fit ℒτk+1\mathcal{L}_{\tau_{k+1}}.

Remark.

This implementation does not require knowing the exact normalizing constant ZτZ_{\tau} in order to evaluate the acceptance probability. It only requires a valid upper bound on the envelope constant BB. Focusing just on TT and ignoring the problem-dependent parameters of B,n,KB,n,K, the total sample complexity is therefore O~​(ln⁡T⋅m)=O~​(ln⁡T⋅ln⁡Nδ)=O~​(ln⁡T⋅ln⁡ln⁡Tδ)\tilde{O}\left(\ln T\cdot m\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\ln T\cdot\ln\frac{N}{\delta}\right)=\widetilde{O}\left(\ln T\cdot\ln\frac{\ln T}{\delta}\right), and we show below that the algorithm fails with probability at most δ\delta.

5.3.2 Relating Temperature to the Precision of Global Optimization

We now find the TT needed to achieve precision 𝔼pT​[d⁡(x)]≤ε\mathbb{E}_{p_{T}}[d(x)]\leq\varepsilon for a given ε\varepsilon, hence casting our sample complexity in more standard terms. Recall we assumed d⁡(x∗)=0d(x^{*})=0.

Lemma 11 (Precision Scaling).

To achieve an expected objective error 𝔼pT​[d⁡(x)]≤ε\mathbb{E}_{p_{T}}[d(x)]\leq\varepsilon, it suffices to set the final temperature to T=O⁡(1/ε)T=O(1/\varepsilon). This implies an overall sample complexity of O~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon).

Proof.

Since d⁡(x)≤Ld2​‖x−x∗‖2d(x)\leq\frac{L_{d}}{2}\|x-x^{*}\|^{2}, taking the expectation over the final target distribution pT​(x)p_{T}(x):

‖x¯T−x∗‖2=‖μ0​x0+T​μd​x∗μ0+T​μd−x∗‖2=2​μ0​Eshift(μ0+T​μd)2=O⁡(1T2).\displaystyle\|\bar{x}_{T}-x^{*}\|^{2}=\left\|\frac{\mu_{0}x_{0}+T\mu_{d}x^{*}}{\mu_{0}+T\mu_{d}}-x^{*}\right\|^{2}=\frac{2\mu_{0}E_{\text{shift}}}{(\mu_{0}+T\mu_{d})^{2}}=O\left(\frac{1}{T^{2}}\right).

To bound the term 𝔼pT​[‖x−x¯T‖2]\mathbb{E}_{p_{T}}[\|x-\bar{x}_{T}\|^{2}], we use Lemma 4. Let qT=𝒩⁡(x¯T,μT−1​In)q_{T}=\mathcal{N}(\bar{x}_{T},\mu_{T}^{-1}I_{n}), where μT=μ0+T​μd\mu_{T}=\mu_{0}+T\mu_{d}. Since pT​(x)≤B​qT​(x)p_{T}(x)\leq Bq_{T}(x) for all xx, we have

𝔼pT​[‖x−x¯T‖2]≤B​𝔼qT​[‖x−x¯T‖2]=n​Bμ0+T​μd=O⁡(1T).\mathbb{E}_{p_{T}}[\|x-\bar{x}_{T}\|^{2}]\leq B\mathbb{E}_{q_{T}}[\|x-\bar{x}_{T}\|^{2}]=\frac{nB}{\mu_{0}+T\mu_{d}}=O\!\left(\frac{1}{T}\right).

For sufficiently large TT, the O⁡(1/T)O(1/T) dominates, so that the error is O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon). Recall that the sample complexity is O~​(ln⁡T⋅ln⁡ln⁡Tδ)\widetilde{O}\left(\ln T\cdot\ln\frac{\ln T}{\delta}\right), which to the higher order multiplicative term is O~​(log⁡1/ε)\widetilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon). ∎

5.4 Comparison to Other Non-convex Optimization Methods

Our sample complexity bound decouples the problem parameters such as dimension nn from the precision ε\varepsilon, yielding a O~​(log⁡1/ε)\tilde{O}(\log 1/\varepsilon) sample complexity, with constants depending on problem parameters. We compare this guarantee with extant methods for non-convex optimization.

1. Grid Search (Lipschitz Optimization): Standard spatial discretization algorithms require O⁡((1/ε)n)O((1/\varepsilon)^{n}) function evaluations, so the precision parameter ε\varepsilon gets exponentially modified.

2. Local MCMC and Simulated Annealing: While local Markov chains scale polynomially in dimension on convex bodies, they can take exponential time in non-convex landscapes. The Holley-Stroock perturbation lemma (Holley and Stroock, 1987) implies escaping a local minimum of depth Δ​E\Delta E at inverse temperature τ\tau requires mixing time O⁡(exp⁡(τ​Δ​E))O(\exp(\tau\Delta E)), and Hajek’s theorem (Hajek, 1988) implies guaranteeing convergence in local MCMC simulated annealing requires a logarithmic cooling schedule τt=O⁡(ln⁡t)\tau_{t}=O(\ln t). These results mean that in the worst case, classical simulated annealing may require O⁡(exp⁡(1/ε))O(\exp(1/\varepsilon)) steps, so again, the precision parameter is exponentially modified.

To mitigate these slow mixing times, classical MCMC and simulated annealing often employ variance-inflated distributions, either as heavier-tailed proposals to guarantee ergodicity (Mengersen and Tweedie, 1996) or as “warm starts” to bound the density ratio between temperature steps (Lovász and Vempala, 2006). However, classical methods utilize variance inflation to aid local random walks, which can take exponentially many samples for non-convex landscapes. In contrast, ALDrIFT adapts the variance-inflation principle to bound the mass coverage of a generative proxy. The proxy dynamically absorbs empirical estimation errors independent of the annealing temperature, allowing the algorithm to achieve logarithmic sample complexity.

3. Deterministic Optimistic Optimization (DOO): Among finite-sample methods, the closest comparators are optimistic partitioning methods such as DOO (Bubeck et al., 2011), SOO (Munos, 2011) and their stochastic/noisy variants (e.g. HOO/StoSOO (Valko et al., 2013) and POO Grill et al. (2015)). In contrast, classical Lipschitz branch-and-bound methods Piyavskii (1972); Shubert (1972) only convergence in different regimes. When the objective is bounded by a quadratic envelope, spatial-partitioning algorithms (Munos, 2011; Bubeck et al., 2011) achieve O~​(log⁡(1/ε))\widetilde{O}(\log(1/\varepsilon)) sample complexity. These methods hierarchically search the space via optimistic estimates of the objective within grid partitions. ALDrIFT achieves this same characteristic rate, but under different trade-offs. Unlike these methods, ALDrIFT requires prior estimates of both the upper and lower bounds on the curvature parameters (μd,Ld\mu_{d},L_{d}), and its sample complexity scales with the full ambient dimension nn, whereas space-partitioning bounds scale with the near-optimality dimension, which could be smaller. Furthermore, extensions like SOO (Munos, 2011) only require the existence of an upper bounding quadratic without needing to know its parameters, a setting ALDrIFT does not handle. Addressing these limitations in ALDrIFT is an exciting direction for future work.

On the other hand, space-partitioning operations are harder to define for discrete, combinatorial, or semantic generative spaces (e.g., sequences generated by LLMs). The ALDrIFT algorithm matches the sample complexity of space partitioning methods for quadratic-bounded functions, while generalizing as an algorithmic framework to other generative priors and discrete optimization objectives whenever Assumption 2 holds.

6 Theoretical Evidence for Coarse Learnability

Complementing the sample complexity proof in Section 5, we now present theoretical evidence to support the coarse learnability assumption (Assumption 2) for simple generative models. First, to demonstrate robustness in the agnostic setting, we prove that a structurally misspecified learner (a single Gaussian) naturally satisfies the coverage condition when approximating a multimodal target (Section 6.1). Second, to validate consistency with classical MBO theory, we show that standard MLE in the realizable setting of MRAS (i.e., exponential families) satisfies the assumption with high probability (Section 6.2). Finally, we demonstrate that coarse learnability extends to a simple Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) task, provided the kernel is deliberately “over-smoothed” to act as a robust coverage envelope (Section 6.3).

6.1 Gaussian Mixtures and Robustness to Mis-specification

Assumption 2 particularly relevant in the agnostic or misspecified setting, where the learner cannot model the complex shape of the target but can learn to cover its support. Indeed, when a lower-capacity model (like a restricted neural network or a single Gaussian) approximates a complex, multimodal target, the MLE objective forces the learner to “spread out” and envelope the target’s support rather than collapsing to a single mode (Minka, 2005). In our setting, the generative model learns to act as this relaxed envelope.

We illustrate this with a Gaussian mixture model target and a single Gaussian learner. Let the target p⁡(x)p(x) be a mixture of kk unit-variance Gaussians:

p⁡(x)=1k​∑i=1k𝒩⁡(μi,1).p(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},1).

Let the learner ℒ\mathcal{L} be restricted to the family of single Gaussians 𝒩⁡(θ,σ2)\mathcal{N}(\theta,\sigma^{2}). This is a mis-specified setting where dTV​(p,ℒ)d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,\mathcal{L}) cannot be made arbitrarily small. However, we show that MLE naturally satisfies Assumption 2.

Theorem 12.

Let the target p⁡(x)=1k​∑i=1k𝒩⁡(μi,1)p(x)=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},1) be a mixture of kk unit-variance Gaussians with means μi∈[−Δ2,Δ2]\mu_{i}\in[-\frac{\Delta}{2},\frac{\Delta}{2}], where Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2. Assume the modes are sufficiently separated such that the population variance satisfies σ∗2≥2\sigma^{*2}\geq 2. Let ℒMLE\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLE}} be the single Gaussian model 𝒩⁡(μ^,σ^2)\mathcal{N}(\hat{\mu},\hat{\sigma}^{2}) learned via MLE on mm i.i.d. samples from pp.

If m=Ω⁡(Δ4​ln⁡(1/δ))m=\Omega(\Delta^{4}\ln(1/\delta)), then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, the learned model satisfies the global coverage condition:

supx∈ℝp⁡(x)ℒMLE​(x)=O⁡(Δ⋅ek):=K.\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}}\frac{p(x)}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MLE}}(x)}=O(\Delta\cdot e^{k}):=K.

Thus, for a fixed number of modes kk, the model family satisfies Assumption 2 with mm scaling polynomially in K=O⁡(Δ)K=O(\Delta) and ln⁡(1/δ)\ln(1/\delta).

Let μ∗\mu^{*} and σ∗2\sigma^{*2} denote the true mean and variance of the target mixture pp.

The mean of the mixture is μ∗=1k​∑μi\mu^{*}=\frac{1}{k}\sum\mu_{i}. The variance of the mixture is given by the law of total variance:

σ∗2=1+1k​∑j=1k(μj−μ∗)2.\sigma^{*2}=1+\frac{1}{k}\sum_{j=1}^{k}(\mu_{j}-\mu^{*})^{2}.

From this identity, we observe that the squared deviation of any single component mean is bounded by the total variance scaled by kk:

(μi−μ∗)2≤∑j=1k(μj−μ∗)2=k⁡(σ∗2−1).(\mu_{i}-\mu^{*})^{2}\leq\sum_{j=1}^{k}(\mu_{j}-\mu^{*})^{2}=k(\sigma^{*2}-1). (5)

By the premise, σ∗2≥2\sigma^{*2}\geq 2. Since the means are bounded in width Δ\Delta, we also have σ∗2≤1+Δ2\sigma^{*2}\leq 1+\Delta^{2}.

The MLE parameters are the sample mean μ^\hat{\mu} and sample variance σ^2\hat{\sigma}^{2}. The target distribution pp is a mixture of Gaussians with bounded parameter support. Since the component means are bounded by Δ/2\Delta/2 and the component variances are fixed at 1, the random variable X∼pX\sim p is sub-Gaussian with norm ‖X‖ψ2=O⁡(Δ)\|X\|_{\psi_{2}}=O(\Delta). Pr⁡(|μ^−μ∗|≥t)≤2​exp⁡(−c​m​t2Δ2).\Pr\left(|\hat{\mu}-\mu^{*}|\geq t\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-cm\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta^{2}}\right).

Pr⁡(|σ^2−σ∗2|≥t)≤2​exp⁡(−c​m​min⁡(t2Δ4,tΔ2)).\Pr\left(|\hat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{*2}|\geq t\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-cm\min\left(\frac{t^{2}}{\Delta^{4}},\frac{t}{\Delta^{2}}\right)\right).

The coverage ratio is r⁡(x)=p⁡(x)ℒ⁡(x)=1k​∑i=1k𝒩⁡(x,μi,1)𝒩⁡(x,μ^,σ^2)r(x)=\frac{p(x)}{\mathcal{L}(x)}=\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{\mathcal{N}(x;\mu_{i},1)}{\mathcal{N}(x;\hat{\mu},\hat{\sigma}^{2})}.
