(μi−μ^)2≤k​V+2​η​k​V+η2.(\mu_{i}-\hat{\mu})^{2}\leq kV+2\eta\sqrt{kV}+\eta^{2}.

Next, consider the denominator 2​(σ^2−1)2(\hat{\sigma}^{2}-1). Using |σ^2−σ∗2|≤η|\hat{\sigma}^{2}-\sigma^{*2}|\leq\eta:

σ^2−1≥σ∗2−1−η=V−η.\hat{\sigma}^{2}-1\geq\sigma^{*2}-1-\eta=V-\eta.

Since we assumed σ∗2≥2\sigma^{*2}\geq 2, we have V≥1V\geq 1. Since η≤0.5\eta\leq 0.5, we have V−η≥V⁡(1−η)≥0.5​VV-\eta\geq V(1-\eta)\geq 0.5V. For small enough constant η\eta, the exponent Ei​(x∗)E_{i}(x^{*}) is bounded by:

Ei​(x∗)≤k​V+2​η​k​V+η22​(V−η)=k2​(1+2​ηk​V+η2k​V1−ηV)≤k.E_{i}(x^{*})\leq\frac{kV+2\eta\sqrt{kV}+\eta^{2}}{2(V-\eta)}=\frac{k}{2}\left(\frac{1+\frac{2\eta}{\sqrt{kV}}+\frac{\eta^{2}}{kV}}{1-\frac{\eta}{V}}\right)\leq k.

Consequently, the maximum value of the component ratio is:

supxTi​(x)=σ^​exp⁡(Ei​(x∗))≤σ^⋅ek.\sup_{x}T_{i}(x)=\hat{\sigma}\exp(E_{i}(x^{*}))\leq\hat{\sigma}\cdot e^{k}.

Since σ^2≤σ∗2+η≤2+Δ2\hat{\sigma}^{2}\leq\sigma^{*2}+\eta\leq 2+\Delta^{2}, we have σ^≤O⁡(Δ)\hat{\sigma}\leq O(\Delta).

Summing over the kk components (each with weight 1/k1/k):

supxp⁡(x)ℒ⁡(x)≤1k​∑i=1ksupxTi​(x)≤1k​∑i=1kO⁡(Δ⋅ek)=O⁡(Δ⋅ek).\sup_{x}\frac{p(x)}{\mathcal{L}(x)}\leq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}\sup_{x}T_{i}(x)\leq\frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k}O(\Delta\cdot e^{k})=O(\Delta\cdot e^{k}).

We can now choose any m≥poly⁡(ln⁡1δ,Δ,ek)m\geq\mathrm{poly}\left(\ln\frac{1}{\delta},\Delta,e^{k}\right) to satisfy Assumption 2. Note that the coverage condition holds globally. ∎

6.2 Exponential Families and Realizable Setting

We now present theoretical justification for coarse learnability for simple distributions. We consider the class of exponential families with a single parameter and show that under benign assumptions on the family, the MLE estimation problem is coarsely learnable. This result extends to some multi-parameter settings, and we present a sketch at the end omitting the details. Note that single-parameter exponential families capture most common distributions such as Gaussian, Exponential, Poisson, Binomial, etc. This result shows that coarse learnability is a natural property of standard statistical estimation in well-behaved settings.

It is important to contextualize the result below within the model reference adaptive search (MRAS) literature. As discussed in Section A.2, standard MRAS utilizes natural exponential families for the parametric model (Hu et al., 2007). While true target distributions are generally complex, analyzing the idealized “realizable” setting, where the target falls within the model family, serves as a theoretical baseline. The analysis below confirms that in this realizable setting, the finite-sample MLE inherently satisfies our coarse learnability assumption. This indicates that our statistical condition is well-grounded, holding for standard parametric families in an idealized realizable setting. Crucially, however, as discussed in Section 6.1, our framework extends guarantees beyond this idealized case to the more general agnostic setting where the target is complex and the model is misspecified, by utilizing the Metropolis–Hastings correction.

Single-Parameter Setting.

Let p⁡(x∣η)=h⁡(x)⋅eη​x−A⁡(η)p(x\mid\eta)=h(x)\cdot e^{\eta x-A(\eta)} be a single-parameter exponential family and let XX denote a random variable following this distribution. Let μ⁡(η)=𝔼X∼p⁡(x∣η)​[X]=A′​(η)\mu(\eta)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p(x\mid\eta)}[X]=A^{\prime}(\eta). We suppose the exponential family satisfies the following simple assumption.

Assumption 3 (Regularity).

We assume the density p⁡(x∣η)p(x\mid\eta) is sub-exponential.44 4 A sub-exponential random variable satisfies Pr[|X|≥K]≤2e−C⋅K\Pr[|X|\geq K]\leq 2e^{-C\cdot K} for all K≥0K\geq 0 and some constant C>0C>0. Further, the true parameter η0\eta_{0} lies in a constant-sized closed interval Ω0\Omega_{0} such that for all η∈Ω0\eta\in\Omega_{0}, we have that A⁡(η)A(\eta) is analytic and 0<vmin≤A′′​(η)≤vmax<∞0<v_{\min}\leq A^{\prime\prime}(\eta)\leq v_{\max}<\infty for some positive constants vmin,vmaxv_{\min},v_{\max}.

The above assumption holds for common distributions such as Gaussian, Bernoulli, Exponential, and Poisson under mild conditions on their parameters. These densities are clearly sub-exponential. Furthermore, we have the following:

Gaussian (with known variance).

We have p(x∣μ)=12​π​σ2e−(x−μ)2/(2σ2)p(x\mid\mu)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}e^{-(x-\mu)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})}. Therefore, η=μ/σ2\eta=\mu/\sigma^{2} and A⁡(η)=η2​σ2/2A(\eta)=\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}/2, so that A′′​(η)=σ2A^{\prime\prime}(\eta)=\sigma^{2}, which is a constant.

Bernoulli.

We have p⁡(x∣μ)=μx​(1−μ)1−xp(x\mid\mu)=\mu^{x}(1-\mu)^{1-x} for x∈{0,1}x\in\{0,1\}. We have η=ln⁡(μ/(1−μ))\eta=\ln(\mu/(1-\mu)), and A⁡(η)=ln⁡(1+eη)=−ln⁡(1−μ)A(\eta)=\ln(1+e^{\eta})=-\ln(1-\mu). We have A′′​(η)=eη/(1+eη)2=μ⁡(1−μ)A^{\prime\prime}(\eta)=e^{\eta}/(1+e^{\eta})^{2}=\mu(1-\mu), which satisfies the above assumption when μ∈[δ,1−δ]\mu\in[\delta,1-\delta] for constant δ>0\delta>0.

Exponential.

We have p⁡(x∣λ)=λ​e−λ​xp(x\mid\lambda)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x} for x≥0x\geq 0. Further, we have η=−λ\eta=-\lambda and A⁡(η)=−ln⁡(−η)A(\eta)=-\ln(-\eta), so that A′′​(η)=1/η2A^{\prime\prime}(\eta)=1/\eta^{2}, which satisfies the above assumption when λ>0\lambda>0 is a constant.

Poisson.

We have p⁡(x∣λ)=e−λ​λx/x!p(x\mid\lambda)=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^{x}/x! for x=0,1,2,…x=0,1,2,\ldots. We have η=ln⁡λ\eta=\ln\lambda, A⁡(η)=eηA(\eta)=e^{\eta}, and A′′​(η)=eη=λA^{\prime\prime}(\eta)=e^{\eta}=\lambda, which satisfies the assumption when λ>0\lambda>0 is a constant.

The derivation of coarse learnability under Assumption 3 uses standard properties of sub-exponential distributions; see, e.g., (Vershynin, 2018) for details. Since we assumed the exponential family is sub-exponential, this means there exist positive constants C1,C2>0C_{1},C_{2}>0 such that for X∼p⁡(x∣η0)X\sim p(x\mid\eta_{0}):

Pr(|X−μ(η0)|>θ)≤C1e−C2⋅θ.\Pr\left(\left|X-\mu(\eta_{0})\right|>\theta\right)\leq C_{1}e^{-C_{2}\cdot\theta}. (6)

This also means (Vershynin, 2018) that there are constants ν2,α\nu^{2},\alpha such that for random variable XX following p⁡(x∣η)p(x\mid\eta), we have:

𝔼⁡[eλ​X]≤eλ2​ν2/2∀|λ|≤1α.\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda X}]\leq e^{\lambda^{2}\nu^{2}/2}\qquad\forall|\lambda|\leq\frac{1}{\alpha}.

Let Z=X−μ⁡(η)Z=X-\mu(\eta), so that 𝔼⁡[Z]=0\mathbb{E}[Z]=0. Clearly, ZZ is also sub-exponential, and satisfies the above equation for some ν2,α\nu^{2},\alpha. Suppose we draw mm samples from p⁡(x∣η)p(x\mid\eta) and let X^\hat{X} be their average:

Pr⁡(X^−μ⁡(η)>ε)=\displaystyle\Pr\left(\hat{X}-\mu(\eta)>\varepsilon\right)= Pr⁡(∑i=1mZi>m⋅ε)=Pr⁡(∏i=1meλ​Zi>em⋅λ⋅ε)\displaystyle\Pr\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}Z_{i}>m\cdot\varepsilon\right)=\Pr\left(\prod_{i=1}^{m}e^{\lambda Z_{i}}>e^{m\cdot\lambda\cdot\varepsilon}\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq (𝔼⁡[eλ​Z])mem⋅λ⋅ε≤em⁡(λ2⋅ν2/2−λ⋅ε).\displaystyle\frac{\left(\mathbb{E}[e^{\lambda Z}]\right)^{m}}{e^{m\cdot\lambda\cdot\varepsilon}}\leq e^{m\left(\lambda^{2}\cdot\nu^{2}/2-\lambda\cdot\varepsilon\right).}

Choosing λ=εν2<1α\lambda=\frac{\varepsilon}{\nu^{2}}<\frac{1}{\alpha} (assuming ε=o⁡(1)\varepsilon=o(1)), we have

Pr⁡(|X^−μ⁡(η)|>ε)≤2​e−m⋅ε22​ν2.\Pr\left(\left|\hat{X}-\mu(\eta)\right|>\varepsilon\right)\leq 2e^{-\frac{m\cdot\varepsilon^{2}}{2\nu^{2}}}.

Choosing ε=m−1/3\varepsilon=m^{-1/3}, this implies:

Pr(|X^−μ(η)|>m−1/3)≤2exp(−m1/32​ν2).\Pr\left(\left|\hat{X}-\mu(\eta)\right|>m^{-1/3}\right)\leq 2\exp\left(-\frac{m^{1/3}}{2\nu^{2}}\right). (7)

We are now ready to show the following theorem, which we show implies Assumption 2.

Theorem 13.

Suppose the exponential family satisfies Assumption 3. Let η^m\hat{\eta}_{m} be the MLE of η0\eta_{0} based on mm samples, satisfying A′​(η^m)=X¯mA^{\prime}(\hat{\eta}_{m})=\bar{X}_{m}, where X¯m\bar{X}_{m} is the average of mm samples. Let ℒ⁡(x)≡p⁡(x∣η^m)\mathcal{L}(x)\equiv p(x\mid\hat{\eta}_{m}). For any small constant γ>0\gamma>0, define

Wm={x:|lnp(x∣η0)−lnp(x∣η^m)|≤m−1/3+γ}.W_{m}=\left\{x:\left|\ln p(x\mid\eta_{0})-\ln p(x\mid\hat{\eta}_{m})\right|\leq m^{-1/3+\gamma}\right\}.

Then, for any m≥poly⁡(vmaxvmin,1ν)m\geq\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{v_{\max}}{v_{\min}},\frac{1}{\nu}\right) and a sufficiently small constant γ>0\gamma>0, with probability 1−2​e−mγ1-2e^{-m^{\gamma}}, the parameter η^m\hat{\eta}_{m} satisfies Pr[X∉Wm]≤e−mγ.\Pr[X\notin W_{m}]\leq e^{-m^{\gamma}}.

Proof.

Let Δ​η=η^m−η0\Delta\eta=\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta_{0}. The log-density ratio is

ℛ⁡(x)=ln⁡p⁡(x∣η0)−ln⁡p⁡(x∣η^m)=(η0−η^m)⋅x+(A⁡(η^m)−A⁡(η0)).\mathcal{R}(x)=\ln p(x\mid\eta_{0})-\ln p(x\mid\hat{\eta}_{m})=(\eta_{0}-\hat{\eta}_{m})\cdot x+(A(\hat{\eta}_{m})-A(\eta_{0})).

Using a Taylor expansion for A⁡(η^m)=A⁡(η0+Δ​η)A(\hat{\eta}_{m})=A(\eta_{0}+\Delta\eta) around η0\eta_{0} up to the second term, for some ξ\xi between η0\eta_{0} and η^m\hat{\eta}_{m}, we have

A⁡(η^m)−A⁡(η0)=A′​(η0)​Δ​η+12​A′′​(ξ)​(Δ​η)2.A(\hat{\eta}_{m})-A(\eta_{0})=A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})\Delta\eta+\frac{1}{2}A^{\prime\prime}(\xi)(\Delta\eta)^{2}.

Substituting this into ℛ⁡(x)\mathcal{R}(x):

ℛ⁡(x)=Δ​η​(A′​(η0)−x)+12​A′′​(ξ)​(Δ​η)2.\mathcal{R}(x)=\Delta\eta(A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})-x)+\frac{1}{2}A^{\prime\prime}(\xi)(\Delta\eta)^{2}.

Let μ⁡(η0)=A′​(η0)\mu(\eta_{0})=A^{\prime}(\eta_{0}) be the true mean. By Eq. 7, the event ℰparam:={|X¯m−μ(η0)|≤m−1/3}\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{param}}:=\{\left|\bar{X}_{m}-\mu(\eta_{0})\right|\leq m^{-1/3}\} occurs with probability at least 1−exp(−m1/3/ν2)1-\exp(-m^{1/3}/\nu^{2}). The MLE satisfies A′​(η^m)=X¯m=μ⁡(η^m)A^{\prime}(\hat{\eta}_{m})=\bar{X}_{m}=\mu(\hat{\eta}_{m}). On ℰparam\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{param}}, we therefore have |A′(η^m)−A′(η0)|≤m−1/3\left|A^{\prime}(\hat{\eta}_{m})-A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})\right|\leq m^{-1/3}. By the Mean Value Theorem, A′​(η^m)−A′​(η0)=A′′​(η∗)​(η^m−η0)A^{\prime}(\hat{\eta}_{m})-A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})=A^{\prime\prime}(\eta^{*})(\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta_{0}) for some η∗\eta^{*} between η0\eta_{0} and η^m\hat{\eta}_{m}. By Assumption 3, A′′​(η∗)≥vmin>0A^{\prime\prime}(\eta^{*})\geq v_{\min}>0. Thus, on ℰparam\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{param}}, we have

|Δη|=|η^m−η0|≤1vmin|A′(η^m)−A′(η0)|≤1vminm−1/3.\left|\Delta\eta\right|=\left|\hat{\eta}_{m}-\eta_{0}\right|\leq\frac{1}{v_{\min}}\left|A^{\prime}(\hat{\eta}_{m})-A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})\right|\leq\frac{1}{v_{\min}}m^{-1/3}.

This implies (Δ​η)2≤m−2/3vmin2(\Delta\eta)^{2}\leq\frac{m^{-2/3}}{v_{\min}^{2}}. Also, on ℰparam\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{param}}, A′′​(ξ)≤vmaxA^{\prime\prime}(\xi)\leq v_{\max} by Assumption 3. This implies the first term Δ​η​(A′​(η0)−x)\Delta\eta(A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})-x) dominates in the equation for ℛ⁡(x)\mathcal{R}(x) when m≥poly⁡(vmaxvmin)m\geq\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{v_{\max}}{v_{\min}}\right). Thus, for |ℛ(x)|≤m−1/3+γ\left|\mathcal{R}(x)\right|\leq m^{-1/3+\gamma}, we require:

|Δη(A′(η0)−x)|≤12m−1/3+γ.\left|\Delta\eta(A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})-x)\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}m^{-1/3+\gamma}.

Since |Δ​η|≤m−1/3vmin\left|\Delta\eta\right|\leq\frac{m^{-1/3}}{v_{\min}}, this requires |A′​(η0)−x|≤12​vmin​mγ:=Km\left|A^{\prime}(\eta_{0})-x\right|\leq\frac{1}{2}v_{\min}m^{\gamma}:=K_{m}. The set WW is then defined by xx such that |x−μ⁡(η0)|≤Km\left|x-\mu(\eta_{0})\right|\leq K_{m}. By Eq. 6, we have Pr[x∉W]=O(e−O⁡(Km))\Pr[x\notin W]=O\left(e^{-O(K_{m})}\right). Choosing γ>0\gamma>0 an appropriately small constant, this completes the proof. ∎

Note that the failure probabilities in the above theorem are monotonically decreasing in mm. Therefore, if we are given K>1,ε>0,δ>0K>1,\varepsilon>0,\delta>0 as in Assumption 2, then we can simply choose a large enough m≥poly⁡(vmaxvmin,1ν,ln⁡1ε​δ)m\geq\mathrm{poly}\left(\frac{v_{\max}}{v_{\min}},\frac{1}{\nu},\ln\frac{1}{\varepsilon\delta}\right) that ensures e−mβ≤min⁡(δ,ε)e^{-m^{\beta}}\leq\min\left(\delta,\varepsilon\right). Further, note that m−1/3+γ<lnKm^{-1/3+\gamma}<\ln K. This ensures that with probability 1−δ1-\delta, we have Pr[p(x|η0)≥K⋅p(x|η^m)]≤ε\Pr\left[p(x|\eta_{0})\geq K\cdot p(x|\hat{\eta}_{m})\right]\leq\varepsilon, hence satisfying Assumption 2.

Multi-Parameter Setting.

Let p⁡(𝐱∣𝜼)=h⁡(𝐱)​exp⁡(𝜼T​𝐱−A⁡(𝜼))p(\mathbf{x}\mid\boldsymbol{\eta})=h(\mathbf{x})\exp(\boldsymbol{\eta}^{T}\mathbf{x}-A(\boldsymbol{\eta})) be a kk-parameter exponential family, where 𝜼∈ℜk\boldsymbol{\eta}\in\Re^{k} and 𝐱∈ℜk\mathbf{x}\in\Re^{k}, and kk being a constant. This for instance, captures multi-dimensional Gaussian distributions with a known covariance matrix, or multinomial distributions. Assuming the resulting density is sub-exponential in the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, it can be shown that such a distribution satisfies Eq. 6 and Eq. 7 with the absolute value replaced by the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, and the constants depending on kk. In particular, the ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm of the deviation from the mean is a sub-exponential random variable. By re-working the same proof as that of Theorem 13, this implies an analog of Theorem 13 to the multi-dimensional setting, under suitable regularity assumptions on A⁡(𝜼)A(\boldsymbol{\eta}). The details are easy to fill in, and omitted.

6.3 Over-smoothed Non-Parametric Estimation

The previous sections demonstrated that coarse learnability arises naturally in parametric settings due to the mass-covering properties of Maximum Likelihood Estimation. We now show that this principle extends to a simple non-parametric Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) task, provided the estimator is deliberately “over-smoothed.”

In classical density estimation, the bandwidth hh of a kernel is typically shrunk as the sample size m→∞m\to\infty to recover the exact target density. However, in our optimization framework, a shrinking bandwidth creates light tails that exponentially under-cover the target’s support, violating Assumption 2. Conversely, if we fix a kernel whose bandwidth dominates the target’s tail decay, the KDE forms a robust coverage envelope. We formalize this in dd-dimensions.

Theorem 14.

Let the target distribution p⁡(x)=𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)p(x)=\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}) be a dd-dimensional isotropic Gaussian. Let ℒKDE​(x)=1m​∑i=1mKh​(x−Xi)\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}K_{h}(x-X_{i}) be the density learned via KDE using a Gaussian kernel Kh(z)=(2πh2)−d/2exp(−∥z∥2/2h2)K_{h}(z)=(2\pi h^{2})^{-d/2}\exp(-\|z\|^{2}/2h^{2}) on mm i.i.d. samples X1,…,XmX_{1},\ldots,X_{m} from pp.

Assume we set the bandwidth to match55 5 The proof easily extends to h=c⋅σh=c\cdot\sigma for constant c≥1c\geq 1. the target’s tail decay, h=σh=\sigma. There exists a universal constant C>0C>0 such that if the sample size satisfies m≥C⁡(d+ln⁡(1/δ))m\geq C(d+\ln(1/\delta)), then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta over the samples, the learned model globally satisfies the coarse learnability condition:

supx∈ℝdp⁡(x)ℒKDE​(x)≤8​ed:=K.\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{p(x)}{\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x)}\leq 8e^{d}:=K.

This implies m=O⁡(ln⁡Kδ)m=O\left(\ln{\frac{K}{\delta}}\right), showing Assumption 2.

Proof.

We first show that for any query point x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, a constant fraction of the empirical samples simultaneously resides near the origin and directionally points toward xx.

Let ℬ={y∈ℝd:‖y‖2≤2​σ2​d}\mathcal{B}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\|y\|^{2}\leq 2\sigma^{2}d\} be the closed ball of radius σ​2​d\sigma\sqrt{2d} centered at the origin. For X∼𝒩⁡(0,σ2​Id)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d}), the expected squared norm is 𝔼⁡[‖X‖2]=σ2​d\mathbb{E}[\|X\|^{2}]=\sigma^{2}d. By Markov’s inequality, the probability that a sample falls outside this ball is bounded by:

Pr⁡(‖X‖2≥2​σ2​d)≤𝔼⁡[‖X‖2]2​σ2​d=12\displaystyle\Pr(\|X\|^{2}\geq 2\sigma^{2}d)\leq\frac{\mathbb{E}[\|X\|^{2}]}{2\sigma^{2}d}=\frac{1}{2}

Thus, the true probability mass of the ball is Pr⁡(X∈ℬ)≥1/2\Pr(X\in\mathcal{B})\geq 1/2.

For any query point x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define the halfspace pointing toward xx as Hx={y∈ℝd:⟨x,y⟩≥0}H_{x}=\{y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle x,y\rangle\geq 0\}. Because the Gaussian distribution is spherically symmetric and centered at the origin, exactly half of the mass of ℬ\mathcal{B} lies in HxH_{x}. Therefore, the true probability that a random sample falls into their intersection is:

px:=Pr⁡(X∈ℬ∩Hx)=12​Pr⁡(X∈ℬ)≥14\displaystyle p_{x}:=\Pr(X\in\mathcal{B}\cap H_{x})=\frac{1}{2}\Pr(X\in\mathcal{B})\geq\frac{1}{4}

We require the empirical fraction of samples in ℬ∩Hx\mathcal{B}\cap H_{x} to tightly concentrate around its true expectation uniformly over all possible directions x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The set of such halfspaces {Hx:x∈ℝd}\{H_{x}:x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\} has VC dimension of dd. Intersecting this class with a fixed set ℬ\mathcal{B} does not increase the VC dimension. By uniform convergence, there exists a universal constant c>0c>0 such that with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta:

supx∈ℝd|1m∑i=1m𝟏{Xi∈ℬ∩Hx}−px|≤cd+ln⁡(1/δ)m\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left|\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\{X_{i}\in\mathcal{B}\cap H_{x}\}}-p_{x}\right|\leq c\sqrt{\frac{d+\ln(1/\delta)}{m}}

We choose the sample size mm sufficiently large such that this uniform error is bounded by 1/81/8. Specifically, this requires m≥C⁡(d+ln⁡(1/δ))m\geq C(d+\ln(1/\delta)) for C=64​c2C=64c^{2}.

Under this condition, with probability 1−δ1-\delta, the empirical fraction of samples falling in ℬ∩Hx\mathcal{B}\cap H_{x} is at least px−1/8≥1/4−1/8=1/8p_{x}-1/8\geq 1/4-1/8=1/8 for all xx simultaneously. Let Sx={Xi:Xi∈ℬ∩Hx}S_{x}=\{X_{i}:X_{i}\in\mathcal{B}\cap H_{x}\} be this subset of samples for a given xx. We are guaranteed that |Sx|≥m/8|S_{x}|\geq m/8 for every x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Conditioned on this uniform convergence event, we evaluate the ratio r⁡(x)=p⁡(x)/ℒKDE​(x)r(x)=p(x)/\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x) for an arbitrary x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. We lower bound the KDE sum by dropping all kernel components except those corresponding to the samples in SxS_{x}:

ℒKDE​(x)=1m​∑i=1mKh​(x−Xi)≥1m​∑Xi∈Sx1(2​π​σ2)d/2​exp⁡(−‖x−Xi‖22​σ2)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}K_{h}(x-X_{i})\geq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{X_{i}\in S_{x}}\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{d/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x-X_{i}\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)

For every Xi∈SxX_{i}\in S_{x}, we know two facts by definition of the set: ‖Xi‖2≤2​σ2​d\|X_{i}\|^{2}\leq 2\sigma^{2}d and ⟨x,Xi⟩≥0\langle x,X_{i}\rangle\geq 0. Expanding the squared distance yields:

‖x−Xi‖2=‖x‖2−2​⟨x,Xi⟩+‖Xi‖2≤‖x‖2+2​σ2​d\displaystyle\|x-X_{i}\|^{2}=\|x\|^{2}-2\langle x,X_{i}\rangle+\|X_{i}\|^{2}\leq\|x\|^{2}+2\sigma^{2}d

Substituting this upper bound on the distance into each kernel exponent in the sum gives:

ℒKDE​(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x) ≥1m​∑Xi∈Sx1(2​π​σ2)d/2​exp⁡(−‖x‖22​σ2)​exp⁡(−d)\displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{m}\sum_{X_{i}\in S_{x}}\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{d/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\exp(-d)
=|Sx|m​1(2​π​σ2)d/2​exp⁡(−‖x‖22​σ2)​exp⁡(−d)\displaystyle=\frac{|S_{x}|}{m}\frac{1}{(2\pi\sigma^{2})^{d/2}}\exp\left(-\frac{\|x\|^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right)\exp(-d)

Because |Sx|≥m/8|S_{x}|\geq m/8 for all xx, we have

ℒKDE​(x)≥18​exp⁡(−d)⋅p⁡(x)⇒supx∈ℝdp⁡(x)ℒKDE​(x)≤8​ed:=K\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x)\geq\frac{1}{8}\exp(-d)\cdot p(x)\qquad\Rightarrow\qquad\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{p(x)}{\mathcal{L}_{\text{KDE}}(x)}\leq 8e^{d}:=K

This completes the proof. ∎

Our proof easily extends to the setting where h=c⋅σh=c\cdot\sigma for constant c≥1c\geq 1 and yields K=O⁡((c​e)d)K=O((ce)^{d}). Further, the same proof idea generalizes to centrally symmetric sub-Gaussian distributions with similar bounds.

7 Empirical Illustration of ALDrIFT versus TopIFT

Although our contributions are primarily theoretical, we present a focused empirical demonstration to validate the necessity of an optimistic, variance-inflated proposal distribution combined with sample correction. We compare ALDrIFT against TopIFT, a baseline that relies on empirical variance without distribution correction and consequently suffers from premature convergence to local optima. While specialized heuristics exist to navigate specific non-convex landscapes, our objective here is not to achieve state-of-the-art empirical performance. Rather, our goal is to cleanly isolate and verify how the core theoretical insights of our framework hold up under strict sample budgets.

Objective Landscape. We study the non-convex optimization setting from Section 5 and define a n=10n=10 dimensional objective d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) characterized by a global quadratic envelope and high-frequency local minima. For x∈ℝ10x\in\mathbb{R}^{10}, let d⁡(x)=μd2​‖x‖2+A​∑i=110(1−cos⁡(ω​xi))d(x)=\frac{\mu_{d}}{2}\|x\|^{2}+A\sum_{i=1}^{10}(1-\cos(\omega x_{i})). The global minimum is located at x∗=𝟎x^{*}=\mathbf{0}. We initialize the prior ℒ0=𝒩⁡(x0,2μ0​In)\mathcal{L}_{0}=\mathcal{N}(x_{0},\frac{2}{\mu_{0}}I_{n}) with x0x_{0} far enough that the optimizer must traverse multiple local optima to succeed. Following the setting in Section 5 assume μd\mu_{d} is known to ALDrIFT as a lower bound on curvature at the optimum solution.

Algorithms. We evaluate both ALDrIFT and TopIFT using a shared sample budget.

  • •

    ALDrIFT (Variance Inflated): We employ the geometric annealing schedule (as described in Section 5), updating the temperature as τk+1=(1+1/n)​τk\tau_{k+1}=(1+1/n)\tau_{k} from an initial τ0=0.1\tau_{0}=0.1 to T=20T=20. At each step, we use Metropolis-Hastings to draw m=200m=200 samples, with a chain length of M=50M=50. Crucially, the model is updated using the inflated variance ℒτ​(x)=𝒩⁡(ω^τ,2μτ​In)\mathcal{L}_{\tau}(x)=\mathcal{N}(\hat{\omega}_{\tau},\frac{2}{\mu_{\tau}}I_{n}), where μτ=μ0+τ​μd\mu_{\tau}=\mu_{0}+\tau\mu_{d} and ω^τ\hat{\omega}_{\tau} is the sample mean.

  • •

    TopIFT (Empirical Variance): The heuristic samples m⋅Mm\cdot M times directly from the current Gaussian model, scores them based on d⁡(x)d(x), selects the top mm samples, and fits the next Gaussian model using their empirical mean and empirical covariance.

Results. Figure 1 (left and center figures) plots the error of the sample mean of the model ℒτ\mathcal{L}_{\tau} as a function of iteration number for two different settings of the parameters, averaged over 1010 runs for each algorithm. TopIFT falls into a sub-optimal local minimum because the elite samples are concentrated in a single valley and the empirical variance shrinks to near-zero. Conversely, ALDrIFT successfully converges close to the global optimum by using an inflated proposal distribution and correcting for it every iteration, empirically validating Theorem 3.

Observe that ALDrIFT converges close to the global optimum, but does not reach it exactly. This occurs because we operate in a highly constrained sampling regime where MM is much smaller than the theoretical requirement for convergence. Consequently, as the temperature increases and the target distribution sharpens, the probability of an accepting M-H transition approaches zero (see Fig. 1, Right). (A similar stalling effect is observed in our LLM experiments in Section 9.) Thus, the primary practical advantage of ALDrIFT lies in its ability to rapidly isolate the global basin of attraction using a limited sample budget. Once there, standard local optimization methods can be applied to precisely locate the exact optimum. This contrasts with TopIFT, which frequently becomes trapped in suboptimal local minima under comparable sample constraints. Conversely, in the asymptotic regime where sample size is unconstrained, naive exploration strategies such as grid search or TopIFT become competitive by brute-forcing the objective landscape, analogous to the asymptotic convergence guarantees of the Cross-Entropy method and MRAS Rubinstein (1999); Hu et al. (2007).

8 Motivating Application: Algorithm-LLM Interaction at Inference-time

One of our motivations for studying MBO with expressive, black-box generative priors comes from algorithm-LLM interaction, specifically via inference-time alignment. Increasingly, real-world combinatorial optimization requires balancing strict global constraints (e.g., graph connectivity, efficiency) with informal, context-dependent local specifications (e.g., scenic preferences, stylistic coherence). While classical algorithms efficiently solve for global feasibility, they are brittle when handling qualitative or ambiguous requirements (Wang et al., 2023). Similarly, while modern LLMs excel at interpreting open-ended requirements Radford et al. (2018); Brown et al. (2020), they consistently struggle to enforce global combinatorial properties. We illustrate this limitation empirically using a cycle detection task. As shown in Figure 2, when asked to find a length-kk cycle in a graph containing a planted cycle, models such as GPT-4, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, and Claude 3.7 Sonnet show rapidly diminishing success rates as the cycle length kk increases. This shows that although models continue to improve rapidly (Gemini Team, 2024; OpenAI, 2024; DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025), their capacity for exact combinatorial search remains bounded by a “short-chain” reasoning frontier.

While this combinatorial reasoning capability can occasionally be improved by fine-tuning a model for a specific global objective (Sanford et al., 2024; Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024), such a tuned model would lose its interpretive flexibility when presented with informal, context-dependent requirements at test time. This trade-off between interpretive flexibility and global optimality arises broadly in domains like robot navigation (Tellex et al., 2011), molecular design, and automated scheduling (Jobson and Li, 2024).

Therefore, problems requiring both interpretive flexibility and enforcement of global constraints exceed the reach of either pure LLMs or pure classical algorithms. For example, in generating a scenic route between two locations, an LLM may expertly evaluate individual route segments for scenic value based on natural language criteria, but it struggles to ensure those segments connect to form a valid, continuous path (Mei et al., 2016). Conversely, a combinatorial algorithm easily ensures path connectivity but cannot interpret the qualitative concept of “scenic-ness.” Similar complementary trade-offs exist in conference planning (Jobson and Li, 2024), where an LLM can semantically analyze abstracts to cluster sessions, but a classical algorithm is required to schedule them into a conflict-free timetable. This interaction is therefore best studied as model-based optimization with expressive black-box generative priors, providing a high-level motivation for the current work.

Within this space, our motivation for MBO comes from inference-time alignment, where a fixed base model is adapted at test time using a reward signal or cost function. Indeed, TopIFT and ALDrIFT are analogous to a test-time training step in LLMs (Sun et al., 2020), in that model fitting (that is, fine-tuning) is performed separately for each problem instance. See also (Huang et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Madaan et al., 2023) for other empirical inference time alignment procedures. Our framework provides complementary theoretical bounds (under the coarse learnability assumption) to this line of work.

9 Empirical Plausibility of Assumption 2

We now present some empirical evidence to support coarse learnability. The rigorous theoretical guarantees established in Section 4 and Section 5 rely on analytic generative models. Given the difficulty with showing corresponding results for algorithm-LLM interaction, we treat the coarse learnability condition (Assumption 2) in this section as an empirical heuristic rather than a provable guarantee. The primary contribution of this work is theoretical, and the goal of these experiments is merely to qualitatively study the empirical dynamics of these models. Specifically, we aim to test whether iterative fitting on a very small number of low-cost samples can heuristically shift an LLM’s distribution in the spirit of coarse learnability, namely, by demonstrating broader coverage over lower-cost regions.

We use a primitive model, GPT-2, since it will demonstrate that our results are not a byproduct of the complex reasoning capabilities of frontier models, and applies to simple models as well. We also use the heuristic algorithm TopIFT (Section 3.1), which does not require estimating the LLM probabilities ℒ⁡(s)\mathcal{L}(s) (Assumption 1) that is required for implementing ALDrIFT. This algorithm has the advantage of being simpler and implementable with frontier models where estimating probabilities directly is harder. We therefore present results for this heuristic, noting that the results for ALDrIFT are comparable and omitted for brevity. Accordingly, these experiments should be interpreted as qualitative evidence for the learnability intuition underlying Assumption 2 for LLMs rather than as an evaluation of ALDrIFT versus TopIFT.

9.1 Line Scheduling

We focus on a simplified line scheduling problem here, and also present results for the low degree spanning tree problem in Section 9.2. In the line scheduling problem, there are KK stations on a line labeled {1,…,K}\{1,\ldots,K\}. For 1≤i<K1\leq i<K, the travel time between station ii and i+1i+1 is tit_{i}. Each station ii has opening time oio_{i}. The user specifies the intervals [ℓi,ui][\ell_{i},u_{i}] for 1≤i≤K1\leq i\leq K that capture the lower bound and the upper bound on how long they wish to spend at each station. The goal is to find a visit duration viv_{i} for each i∈{1,…,K}i\in\{1,\ldots,K\} that specifies how much time the user should spend at each station; let v→\vec{v} be the vector of these durations. If the user reaches a station before time oio_{i}, then they need to wait there until time oio_{i}. We constrain all numbers, including those generated by the LLM, to be integers.

We split the problem constraints between a combinatorial algorithm that provides zeroth-order feedback on the objective d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) and the LLM as follows.

Algorithm’s Constraints.

Given a solution v→\vec{v}, for i≥2i\geq 2, let aia_{i} be the arrival time at station ii, and wiw_{i} be the waiting time for the station to open; we assume w1=o1=0w_{1}=o_{1}=0. The total wait time is d⁡(v→)=∑i=1Kwid(\vec{v})=\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}, and this is the algorithm’s cost (or objective function).

LLM’s Constraints.

The LLM’s constraints correspond to the visit time intervals [ℓi,ui][\ell_{i},u_{i}] for each point ii. Its cost is the total violation of the visit time computed as ∑i=1Kηi\sum_{i=1}^{K}\eta_{i}, where ηi\eta_{i} is the distance of the visit time viv_{i} from the interval [ℓi,ui][\ell_{i},u_{i}]. This quantity is 00 if vi∈[ℓi,ui]v_{i}\in[\ell_{i},u_{i}].

The LLM (GPT-2) is initially fine-tuned to satisfy only the local visit duration intervals, making it “oblivious” to the global waiting time constraint. This yields the model ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}. We generate instances with K=10K=10 and where each ti,ℓi,uit_{i},\ell_{i},u_{i} is an integer in the range [1,20][1,20] with the constraint ℓi≤ui\ell_{i}\leq u_{i}. For i≥2i\geq 2, we set oi=oi−1+ti−1+ui−1,o_{i}=o_{i-1}+t_{i-1}+u_{i-1}, so that there is a solution with wait time 00 if we set vi≥uiv_{i}\geq u_{i} for each ii. The only solution among these that also has a visit time violation 00 is the solution that sets vi=uiv_{i}=u_{i} for each ii.

In our experiment, we will consider the specific instance where the visit time bounds are set as ℓi=1\ell_{i}=1 and ui=20u_{i}=20, hence being vacuous, and all travel times are set to ti=10t_{i}=10. For this instance, the optimal visit time vector is ⟨20,…,20⟩\langle 20,\ldots,20\rangle, and this vector has wait time zero and visit time violation of 00. If the visit time at a station is v<20v<20, then the solution has to wait 20−v20-v steps before the next station opens.

In Figure 3(a), we show the box plot, for 2020 runs of the algorithm, of the algorithm’s cost (total wait time) for the Best-of-LLM baseline that draws NN samples from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} and outputs the solution with minimum cost d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot). We plot this for N=1N=1 and N=400N=400 samples. Note that the median algorithm’s cost for Best-of-LLM for N=400N=400 is at least 100100. We observe that for any station, if vv is the visit time assigned to the station in a sample from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}, then assuming this is a uniform distribution on [1,20][1,20], we would have 𝔼⁡[v]=10.5\mathbb{E}[v]=10.5, so that the expected wait time is (20−𝔼⁡[v])⋅(K−1)=85.5(20-\mathbb{E}[v])\cdot(K-1)=85.5. This roughly agrees with the baseline. Further note that Pr[v=20]≤0.05\Pr[v=20]\leq 0.05. This is because the LLM is initially only aware of the bound v∈[0,20]v\in[0,20], and hence, is likely to choose an integer visit time uniformly at random from this range. It is unaware of the global waiting time constraint. Assuming the dimensions behave independently, this means Pr[Wait time =0]≤10−10\Pr[\mbox{Wait time }=0]\leq 10^{-10}, so that merely sampling from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} is very unlikely to find a solution with optimal waiting time.

We then compare this to TopIFT (Section 3.1) that fine-tunes ℒ\mathcal{L} iteratively using zeroth-order feedback about d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot). For TopIFT, we set the parameters as m=4m=4, M=12M=12, and Q=8Q=8, so that the total number of samples used is comparable to N=400N=400 used by the baseline. We consider 2020 independent runs of the algorithm, and in Figure 3(a), we show the Box plot of the best waiting time obtained after rr iterations of the outer loop of TopIFT. Though the Best-of-LLM baseline yields waiting time (objective d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot)) of at least 100100 even with N=400N=400 samples, we note that TopIFT improves on this even with r=4r=4, generating the optimal visit-time vector almost always (wait time = 0) at r=8r=8 iterations.

In Figure 3(b), we show, for one run of the algorithm, the distribution of the m⋅M=48m\cdot M=48 samples generated by the model Lr−1L_{r-1} for 1≤r≤81\leq r\leq 8, and the distribution of the best m=4m=4 samples (according to the algorithm’s cost) among these used for fine-tuning LrL_{r}. Note that initially the fine-tuning samples move the model only slightly, while in later iterations the fine-tuned model produces solutions with substantially lower algorithmic cost than the fine-tuning data itself. Thus, the update is not merely memorizing the elite set, but shifting the model’s distribution further toward the low-cost region. This behavior is qualitatively analogous to Assumption 2: a learner trained on a small sample from a target distribution produces a proposal that covers that target directionally better than the raw sample alone would suggest.66 6 We note that the same effect cannot be observed with only one round of fine-tuning — if we set Q=1Q=1, m=30m=30, and M=12M=12, and take the best waiting time of the samples from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} and 4040 samples from ℒ1\mathcal{L}_{1} (so that the total number of samples remains 400400), we observe the waiting time is 8181. This shows the advantage of the iterated framework. While Figure 3(b) does not verify the density-ratio conclusion of Assumption 2, it provides empirical evidence for the kind of coarse, mass-covering extrapolation that the assumption posits.

This phenomenon, where the model collapses to the optimal solution (Shumailov et al., 2024) demonstrates a remarkable ability of the LLM to extrapolate beyond the limited fine-tuning data. The iterative guidance from the zeroth-order feedback, even with a small sample size, enables the LLM to learn complex combinatorial constraints that it was initially unaware of.

9.2 Low Degree Spanning Tree

In the low degree spanning tree problem, the input is a graph with n=16n=16 vertices numbered 0,1,…,150,1,\ldots,15. We start by including the Hamiltonian path that includes all edges of the form (i,i+1)(i,i+1) for i∈{0,1,…,14}i\in\{0,1,\ldots,14\}. Next, for every pair of vertices, we add an edge between this pair with probability p=0.4p=0.4, removing duplicates. Note that the expected degree of a vertex lies in [6,8][6,8], and the graph has approximately 6060 edges in expectation.

The goal is to output a spanning tree minimizing the number of vertices with degree larger than two; in the ideal case, a Hamiltonian path. We split this problem between a combinatorial algorithm that captures the objective d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot) and LLM as follows:

Algorithm’s Cost.

The algorithm simply wants to output a spanning tree. Given a solution xx as a list of edges, its cost d⁡(x)d(x) is the number of connected components induced by xx minus 11, so that the optimal cost is 00, and the maximum possible cost is n−1=15n-1=15.

LLM’s Cost.

These correspond to the local node-wise degree constraints. We measure the cost of the LLM’s solution (set of edges) as the number of vertices whose degree is greater than 22.

We fine-tune GPT-2 on forests with maximum degree two, yielding the base model ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0}. We then run the TopIFT heuristic (Section 3.1) with m=4m=4, M=50M=50, and Q=3Q=3. Note that the total number of samples is N=m⋅M⋅Q=600N=m\cdot M\cdot Q=600. We compare to two baselines: In the Best-of-ALG baseline, we generate NN random spanning trees (all with cost d⁡(⋅)=0d(\cdot)=0) and compute the probability assigned by ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} to each of them, choosing the best one. In the Best-of-LLM baseline, we generate NN solutions from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} and score them according to the cost d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot), choosing the best one.

In Fig. 4, we illustrate the solutions found for a specific random test instance by the different baselines and TopIFT. Note that samples from ℒ0\mathcal{L}_{0} satisfy the degree constraints, but are disconnected. Best-of-LLM for N=600N=600 (Fig. 4(c)) improves connectivity but still finds a solution that is not only disconnected, but has degree violations. On the other hand, TopIFT finds a Hamiltonian path77 7 This does not happen for all 1515 test instances; however, TopIFT finds one connected component in all instances., hence achieving optimum cost for both the algorithm and LLM. Finally, note that random spanning trees (Fig. 4(e)), though connected, have many degree violations. (The latter is also essentially what Best-of-ALG for N=1N=1 and N=600N=600 generate.) This visually shows that TopIFT is incorporating both the algorithm’s and the LLM’s constraints in a non-trivial fashion, indeed, finding the “optimum” solution on this instance. This showcases the power of the LLM in learning a complicated combinatorial constraint from a few samples, which aligns with coarse learnability.

10 Conclusion

Our framework opens exciting avenues for future research. An ideal goal would be to prove a condition akin to coarse learnability for general LLMs, and a particularly compelling direction is to formally characterize the class of coarse learners and determine under what conditions modern LLMs fall into this category. For instance, which architectural features, training regimes, or fine-tuning strategies enable these models to satisfy the coarse learnability assumption? Addressing this question may require synthesizing insights from recent work on transformers and chain-of-thought reasoning through the lens of circuit complexity (Merrill and Sabharwal, 2024). Another direction is to explore more powerful optimization oracles, such as those providing gradients of the log-probability, which could enable the use of Langevin MCMC in place of Metropolis–Hastings, potentially enhancing the efficiency and scalability of the framework. Finally, it would be interesting to extend Section 5 to work with weaker assumptions than quadratic bounding, and to extend ALDrIFT to remove Assumption 1. Collectively, these directions suggest a rich landscape for integrating statistical learning theory with combinatorial optimization, pointing toward a principled foundation for adaptive generative models.

Appendix A Additional Discussion on ALDrIFT and Coarse Learnability

A.1 Connecting TopIFT to ALDrIFT

Recall TopIFT from Section 3.1. We now describe a smooth approximation of TopIFT that avoids the hard selection of the mm smallest-cost samples, and show that this naturally leads to a procedure akin to ALDrIFT.

Towards this end, we position TopIFT within a framework in which the algorithm tries to make the distribution ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} a progressively good approximation to the distribution pT∗p_{T}^{*}. Unfortunately, obtaining a closed form for ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} in TopIFT seems difficult because we choose the samples with the smallest d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot), i.e., hard-min. To circumvent this difficulty, we will use a soft-min distribution to approximate this step; this leads to a simulated annealing algorithm that we describe next.

Note that the construction of Sr′S^{\prime}_{r} in Section 3.1 can be split into two steps:

  1. 1.

    We generate ss from the distribution ℒr−1\mathcal{L}_{r-1}. If this is repeated m⋅Mm\cdot M times, this corresponds to generating SrS_{r}.

  2. 2.

    We select the samples from SrS_{r} with a minimum d⁡(⋅)d(\cdot). This can be smoothly approximated by keeping each s∈Srs\in S_{r} with probability e−τr⋅d(s)e^{-\tau_{r}\cdot d(s)}. This is a “soft-min” that favors solutions ss with smaller d⁡(s)d(s). The parameter τr\tau_{r} can be chosen so that if D=maxs∈S⁡d⁡(s)D=\max_{s\in S}d(s), then τr=ln⁡MD\tau_{r}=\frac{\ln M}{D}. This ensures that any s∈Ss\in S is sub-selected in this step with probability at least 1M\frac{1}{M}, so that 𝔼⁡[|Sr′|]≥m\mathbb{E}[|S^{\prime}_{r}|]\geq m.

Therefore, the sampling distribution of Sr′S^{\prime}_{r} is proportional to ℒr−1(s)⋅e−τr⋅d(s)\mathcal{L}_{r-1}(s)\cdot e^{-\tau_{r}\cdot d(s)}. If we assume that ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} is faithfully learned from these samples, we obtain ℒr(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−∑t=1rτt⋅d(s)\mathcal{L}_{r}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-\sum_{t=1}^{r}\tau_{t}\cdot d(s)}. We can now choose the number of iterations QQ so that ∑t=1Qτt≈T\sum_{t=1}^{Q}\tau_{t}\approx T, which leads to the distribution pTp_{T}. This yields a smoothed variant of TopIFT, analogous to simulated annealing, where the temperature τ=∑t=1rτt\tau=\sum_{t=1}^{r}\tau_{t} is gradually increased across iterations and a model pτp_{\tau} is learned. The gradual increase ensures that the set Sr′S^{\prime}_{r} at each iteration remains sufficiently large.

A key challenge is that in each iteration, the model ℒr\mathcal{L}_{r} only approximates the sampling distribution Sr′S^{\prime}_{r}. This approximation can be quite crude, since the distribution pτ(s)∝ℒ(s)⋅e−τ⋅d(s)p_{\tau}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}(s)\cdot e^{-\tau\cdot d(s)} encodes combinatorial constraints that the model cannot fully capture, even with many samples. Consequently, errors can accumulate multiplicatively across fine-tuning iterations, making it difficult to formally prove convergence for the simple heuristic. We address this issue by incorporating a Metropolis–Hastings step to select the top samples. This allows the approximately learned model ℒr−1\mathcal{L}_{r-1} to serve as an efficient proposal distribution, while the acceptance rule ensures sampling from the true target distribution pτp_{\tau}, preventing error accumulation. This leads to the ALDrIFT algorithm.

A.2 ALDrIFT vis–a–vis Model Reference Adaptive Search (MRAS)

Our analysis of ALDrIFT can be interpreted as a finite-sample robustification of the model reference adaptive search (MRAS) framework (Hu et al., 2007) via the Metropolis–Hastings proposal step. In the MRAS framework, one defines a sequence of ideal target distributions, gk​(s)g_{k}(s), and updates a parametric model f⁡(⋅,θk)f(\cdot;\theta_{k}) to approximate gkg_{k} by minimizing the KL-divergence DKL(gk∥fθ)D_{\text{KL}}(g_{k}\|f_{\theta}). In our instantiation, gk​(s)∝ℒ0​(s)​e−τk​d​(s)g_{k}(s)\propto\mathcal{L}_{0}(s)e^{-\tau_{k}d(s)}.

Standard MRAS theory guarantees f⁡(⋅,θk)f(\cdot;\theta_{k}) converges to a point mass at the globally optimal solution for dd. However, this analysis relies both on exactly updating the parameter θ\theta via infinite samples as well as the specific structural properties of natural exponential families to ensure the optimum always remains within the support of this generated distributions (Hu et al., 2007). Therefore, this theory does not provide explicit sample complexity bounds. In the finite-sample regime, projecting a complex target pτp_{\tau} onto a generative model introduces empirical errors. Without specific statistical guarantees, there is no assurance that a polynomial number of samples suffices to maintain coverage of the optimal region, and as mentioned before, this aspect may break the algorithm.

Our framework identifies the statistical assumption (coarse learnability) and algorithmic modification (utilizing the coarse generative model as a proposal for Metropolis–Hastings rather than sampling from it directly) needed for achieving polynomial sample complexity in classical MBO. While methods like MRAS rely on the rigid geometry of exponential families to guarantee support preservation, Assumption 2 requires that the learner captures the target’s mass within a polynomial factor. Our framework therefore shifts the burden from architectural correctness (choosing the right parametric family) to statistical expressivity (learning a cover), making the theory applicable to settings where exact parametric alignment is impossible. We presented a simple case of such model mis-match in Section 6.1.
